Homogeneous coordinates and perspective division

Homogeneous coordinates and perspective division

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

Phase 7 derives the affine block matrix, distinguishes a singular affine map from an invertible frame, and traces model → view → homogeneous clip → NDC using a declared projection. The worked figure keeps the divisor visible and checks the chosen near/far depth endpoints.

An affine homogeneous point has last coordinate one; a direction has zero. Nonzero common scale defines projective equivalence, while dehomogenization divides by a nonzero final component. Clip representatives and projective classes have related but distinct semantics.

(2,4,6,2)(2,4,6,2) and (1,2,3,1)(1,2,3,1) describe one finite projective point. NDC normalization standardizes ranges, not vector length.

Prerequisites

  • Vectors coordinates and affine points — Point, displacement and coordinate roles determine which geometric operations are meaningful.

Used by

  • Linear affine and projective transformations

Later curriculum sources can deepen this same node; no future coverage is marked complete. - Ray-triangle intersection - Camera calibration and bundle adjustment

  • Homogeneous clipping and perspective interpolation
  • Position reconstruction from depth
  • Camera gauge freedoms and observability

Recall and next depth

Explain why perspective division is nonlinear and why clipping must precede casual division. Full production proofs, target-specific integration and learner mastery require further evidence.

University course development

Extend the existing account with the geometric reason for the final divide. A 3D point is stored as (x,y,z,1)(x,y,z,1); after multiplying by a projective matrix it becomes (X,Y,Z,W)(X,Y,Z,W). Dividing the first three components by WW maps the homogeneous representative to ordinary coordinates. Any nonzero scalar multiple of a homogeneous vector represents the same point, which is why this division is meaningful. For a perspective camera, WW is chosen to depend on depth, so apparent size shrinks with distance. A direction has homogeneous coordinate zero and is not translated like a point. Projection matrices encode the camera frustum before division; afterward, a viewport transform scales and shifts normalized coordinates to pixels and commonly flips the vertical axis because image rows increase downward. Keep clipping before division to avoid unstable behavior around W=0W=0.

Coordinate frames, transformations, and pose · Cameras, projection, and calibration

Phase 11 camera development

Homogeneous image coordinates represent a ray up to nonzero scale; perspective division produces normalized image coordinates. Monocular reconstruction has a separate physical scale gauge: multiplying all scene points and camera translations by the same positive factor preserves projections. Do not confuse representational scale with unknown metric scale. A known object dimension, baseline, or depth measurement can anchor metres; normalizing a homogeneous vector cannot. This assumes calibrated perspective projection without an external scale prior. The distinction explains why a numerically precise reconstruction can still lack physical units. Dot products and orthogonality

Dot products and orthogonality

Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: Phase6

Definition and mechanism

An inner product provides a scalar measurement of two vectors. In orthonormal real coordinates the dot is a sum of component products. Its geometric form is length product times angle cosine. Orthogonality means zero inner product; zero itself has no angle.

(3,4,0)⋅(2,0,0)=6(3,4,0)\cdot(2,0,0)=6, while the cosine is 6/(5⋅2)=0.66/(5\cdot2)=0.6. Coordinate dotting assumes the correct metric.

Prerequisites

  • Norms lengths and induced distances — Lengths and their domains are needed before unit directions or angular measurements.

Camera view and clip-space pipeline

Camera view and clip-space pipeline

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase7 · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

A camera pose maps camera coordinates to world coordinates; its inverse is the view map. Projection produces homogeneous clip coordinates, clipping applies the API-specific inequalities, and valid perspective division produces NDC. Storage order supplies none of these coordinate contracts.

Reconstruction cue: A standard minus-Z perspective example needs a point in front of the camera and a meaningful clip w before division.

Continuous explanation · Coverage and source gap · Sources and verification

University course development

Extend the existing transform pipeline with the clipping and depth-precision decisions that make projection robust. A view frustum is the set of points a camera can see, bounded by near and far planes as well as image sides. Transforming the frustum into a canonical clip cube makes outside tests cheap; partially intersecting triangles must be clipped and triangulated so the rasterizer still receives triangles. The near plane also avoids geometry crossing the eye plane, while the far plane limits depth range. Floating-point depth values are unevenly distributed after perspective division, so an excessively tiny near distance paired with a huge far distance can make two nearby surfaces quantize to the same depth and produce z-fighting. Choose the narrowest useful depth interval and keep the view, clip, normalized, and screen coordinates distinct.

A scene description becomes an image · Cameras, projection, and calibration · Rasterization, coverage, and depth

Phase 11 camera development

A raster-to-ray camera maps a pixel to a geometric sample; In a pinhole model, invert projection and view transforms to recover a camera-space direction, then transform it to world space without applying translation as if it were a point. Pixel-center convention, viewport origin, handedness, clip-depth range, and normalization all affect the result. Offset a pixel to generate differential rays and estimate the surface footprint; that footprint grows with depth and changes with surface orientation. Keep ray generation distinct from raster projection while ensuring their conventions agree. Link: A camera model must close the loop; research: Four deeper links from the TUM lecture review.

Ownership and non-owning views

Ownership and non-owning views

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C003 · Latest development: C010

Definition and mechanism

By-value copies use member semantics, not recursive deep cloning. Rule-Zero composition delegates ownership to members; raw owners must coordinate transfer and release. Copying a pointer/view/handle is not acquiring ownership.

Copying span/string_view or capturing a view by value copies only a descriptor. An owning string capture supplies independent storage; a view or handle does not automatically pin a deferred resource.

The inline C++ laboratory distinguishes NamedVector::to_array, which copies values into a new array, from ArrayVector::view, which aliases actual array elements without owning them. Neither span nor pointer extends backing lifetime. Ownership and RAII are introduced as next-depth connections, not yet a full exception-safety treatment.

M010 makes the distinction operational: an owner is responsible for release; a borrow only accesses. std::unique_ptr expresses exclusive ownership, std::shared_ptr retains a shared lifetime, and std::weak_ptr observes without extending that lifetime. Smart pointers do not remove the borrow/invalidation rules of raw pointers obtained from them. See RAII and resource handles and Exclusive and shared smart-pointer ownership.

An owner controls a resource’s validity and release; a view merely refers to it. Vector owns its element buffer; span does not copy or prolong that buffer’s life. Owner destruction or invalidating reallocation can dangle the span. A reader retaining a span needs stable live backing for every read, not only at construction.

Prerequisites

  • Storage duration and object lifetime — Access requires an object and backing storage that are still valid.
  • Dynamic allocation and heap — Allocated buffers/blocks supply the storage whose ownership and fragmentation matter.

Used by

  • Memory-mapped files — uses this mechanism as stated in its prerequisites.
  • Atomic publication and durability — uses this mechanism as stated in its prerequisites.
  • Deferred captures and borrowed views
  • Copy semantics and resource identity
  • Rules of Three Five and Zero
  • RAII and resource handles
  • Exclusive and shared smart-pointer ownership

Pending: smart owners, shared immutable data and scheduling/resource pinning.

BVH build traversal and workload selection

BVH build, traversal, and workload selection

A bounding-volume hierarchy is a tree whose nodes bound groups of primitives. Its purpose is not to make intersection magically faster; it is to let a query prove that large groups cannot matter.

For an overlap query Q, traversal follows a simple implication:

if Q does not overlap node.bounds, then Q cannot overlap any primitive below that node.

That pruning claim is only correct when every child primitive is actually contained by every ancestor bound. Tree construction therefore owns an invariant: each internal bound is the union of its children, and each leaf bound contains the primitives assigned to the leaf.

Build choices

A median split sorts or partitions primitive centroids and divides them into similarly sized groups. It is simple and usually avoids catastrophically unbalanced trees, but equal primitive counts do not imply equal traversal cost.

Surface-area heuristic construction estimates expected query/ray work. In the common ray-tracing interpretation, a split cost has the form

C=CT+ALAPNLCI+ARAPNRCI, C = C_T + \frac{A_L}{A_P}N_L C_I + \frac{A_R}{A_P}N_R C_I,

where APA_P is parent surface area, AL,ARA_L,A_R are child areas, NL,NRN_L,N_R are primitive counts, CTC_T is traversal cost and CIC_I is primitive-intersection cost. Binned SAH approximates candidate split positions efficiently.

LBVH chooses hierarchy structure from Morton ordering. It can build quickly and map well to parallel hardware, but tree quality can be worse than a careful SAH build for some scenes. Which strategy wins depends on how often the scene rebuilds and how expensive later queries are.

Traversal representation

A production BVH must choose node layout as deliberately as split policy. Questions include:

  • binary versus wider nodes;
  • array indices versus pointers;
  • parent links or stackless encodings;
  • leaf primitive ranges;
  • AoS versus SoA bounds;
  • quantized bounds;
  • traversal stack depth and overflow behavior;
  • child ordering by query direction or distance.

For GPU traversal, divergence and memory coalescing can dominate the nominal tree complexity.

Dynamic scenes

Refitting recomputes ancestor bounds without changing topology. It is cheap when objects move modestly, but tree quality can decay. Rebuilding restores quality at higher cost. A useful dynamic policy measures a quality proxy and rebuilds when continued bad traversal is more expensive than reconstruction.

Dynamic AABB trees instead maintain a mutable hierarchy and often enlarge leaf bounds by a motion margin. The margin trades fewer reinserts for more false candidates.

Executable reference

tools/labs/spatial_index_lab.cpp builds a median-split BVH over deterministic random AABBs and compares 250 overlap queries against a brute-force oracle. Any missed or extra primitive is a test failure. The same laboratory also contains A* graph search with relaxation, reinsertion and unreachable-goal handling.

The witness does not claim SAH quality, LBVH construction, dynamic updates, SIMD traversal, ray packet behavior, navmesh construction, or KairoSpatial parity. Those remain separate evidence layers.

Related: AABB overlap and containment, Prefix scan and stream compaction, Field reordering and AoS versus SoA.

SAH, Morton and refit witness

tools/labs/bvh_sah_refit_lab.cpp advances the construction side beyond the earlier median-split query oracle. It computes prefix/suffix bounds for candidate partitions and minimizes the surface-area-weighted primitive cost, verifies that two separated three-object clusters split between the clusters, tests 3D Morton bit interleaving on a controlled monotone coordinate sweep, and refits a parent bound after one child moves.

This is enough to make the equations executable, but not enough to call the builder a production binned SAH or LBVH. A complete next layer needs fixed-bin accumulation, stable primitive partitioning, LBVH range/split construction from Morton prefixes, dynamic-tree rotations or reinsertion, and measured build-versus-query trade-offs on real workloads.

A star search and navigation contracts

A* search and navigation contracts

A* is Dijkstra-style relaxation ordered by an estimate of the remaining cost. For node n,

f(n)=g(n)+h(n), f(n)=g(n)+h(n),

where g(n)g(n) is the best path cost currently known from the start and h(n)h(n) estimates the cost from n to the goal.

The algorithm is not “put nodes in a priority queue and stop when the goal first appears.” Correctness depends on the edge-cost domain, heuristic assumptions, stale queue entries, and whether improved paths are allowed to reopen nodes.

With nonnegative edge costs and a zero heuristic, A* becomes Dijkstra’s algorithm. That is a useful oracle mode. An admissible heuristic never overestimates the true remaining cost; a consistent heuristic additionally satisfies a triangle-like condition and simplifies closed-set reasoning.

Relaxation

For edge n → m with cost c,

gcandidate=g(n)+c. g_{candidate}=g(n)+c.

If this is smaller than the currently known g(m)g(m), update g(m)g(m), remember n as m’s parent, and push a new queue item. Priority queues commonly keep stale older entries; when popped, compare the queued score with the latest stored score and discard stale work.

A design that permanently closes a node before the heuristic assumptions justify that decision can return a suboptimal path.

Navigation is larger than A*

A navigation system also needs a graph construction story. For a navmesh this includes walkable geometry, polygon adjacency, portals, agent radius/height constraints, dynamic obstacle policy and a path-smoothing or funnel stage. A* only solves the discrete shortest-path problem on the graph it is given.

Executable reference

tools/labs/spatial_index_lab.cpp includes an A* implementation and tests a weighted graph using h = 0, making the expected result equivalent to Dijkstra’s optimum. It also checks an unreachable goal.

The witness does not yet prove navmesh generation, admissible geometric heuristics, funnel smoothing, dynamic replanning, hierarchical navigation or KairoSpatial parity.

Bounding volume hierarchies

Bounding volume hierarchies

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

A bounding volume hierarchy (BVH) organizes primitives into a tree of enclosing boxes. An internal node’s box contains the boxes of its children; a leaf stores a small set of triangles. To trace a ray, test the root box, recurse only into intersected children, and compare triangle hits in reached leaves. A box miss safely rejects every primitive beneath it, so the hierarchy reduces expensive exact tests when geometry is spatially coherent. Construction chooses how to group primitives and where to split; a surface-area heuristic estimates expected traversal work, while simpler median splits are faster to build. Dynamic scenes may refit boxes after deformation or rebuild the hierarchy when overlap grows. Correctness requires every primitive to remain enclosed; performance depends on tree quality and ray distribution.

Prerequisites

  • Ray-triangle intersection
  • Manifold polygon meshes and boundary structure

Used by

  • Worlds, Images and Inference

  • Radiance fields and Gaussian splatting ## Full teaching explanation

Center of mass and inertia

Center of mass and inertia

The center of mass is the point at which translational motion can be separated cleanly from rotational motion for a rigid body.

For point masses mim_i at positions rir_i,

rcm=1M∑imiri,M=∑imi. r_{cm}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_i m_i r_i, \qquad M=\sum_i m_i.

For a continuous density ρ(r)\rho(r),

rcm=1M∫rρ(r)dV. r_{cm}=\frac{1}{M}\int r\rho(r)\,dV.

A visual pivot, modeling origin or collider-local origin does not have to equal the center of mass.

Inertia tensor

Relative to center of mass, the inertia tensor is

I=∫(∥r∥2𝟏−rr𝖳)dm. I= \int \left( \|r\|^2\mathbf{1}-rr^{\mathsf T} \right)dm.

It maps angular velocity to angular momentum in body coordinates:

L=Iω L=I\omega

when the tensor and vector are expressed in compatible frames.

In world space, if body orientation is rotation RR,

Iworld=RIbodyR𝖳, I_{world}=RI_{body}R^{\mathsf T},

and similarly for the inverse inertia when invertible.

Parallel-axis theorem

Moving the reference point away from the center of mass changes inertia:

IP=Icm+M(∥d∥2𝟏−dd𝖳), I_P= I_{cm} + M\left( \|d\|^2\mathbf{1}-dd^{\mathsf T} \right),

where dd is the displacement between reference points.

This is why using a collider-origin inertia as though it were a center-of-mass inertia couples translation and rotation incorrectly.

Scaling

Changing units does not change the physical body. Numerically converting metres to centimetres changes coordinate values and unit labels consistently.

Physically resizing a uniform-density object does change mass and inertia. Under uniform length scale ss in 3D at fixed density, mass scales as s3s^3 and inertia as s5s^5.

Impulse coupling

An impulse JJ at lever arm rr changes angular velocity by

Δω=Iworld−1(r×J). \Delta\omega=I^{-1}_{world}(r\times J).

This feeds directly into contact effective mass and constraint solving.

Read the connected explanation in Continuous Notes/Game Engine - From First Frame to Living Worlds#From the push on a panel to a repeatable rigid-body simulator.

Related: Impulse and force timing, Mass properties and inertia tensor.

Impulse and force timing

Impulse and force timing

Force and impulse are related but they belong to different timing contracts.

Force is a rate of momentum change:

F=dpdt. F=\frac{dp}{dt}.

Impulse integrates force over time:

J=∫t0t1F(t)dt=Δp. J=\int_{t_0}^{t_1}F(t)\,dt = \Delta p.

For constant mass and a linear impulse applied directly to the center of mass,

Δv=M−1J. \Delta v=M^{-1}J.

There is no additional timestep factor when applying an impulse that is already an integrated momentum change. Multiplying by Δt\Delta t again turns the update into the wrong units.

For a force held constant through a numerical step,

J≈FΔt, J\approx F\Delta t,

so the timestep enters when converting the force into an approximate impulse.

Off-centre impulse

An impulse at world-space point pp relative to center of mass xx has lever arm

r=p−x. r=p-x.

Angular impulse is

ΔL=r×J. \Delta L=r\times J.

With world inverse inertia I−1I^{-1},

Δω=I−1(r×J). \Delta\omega=I^{-1}(r\times J).

A contact solver uses this coupling when computing the effective mass seen along a contact direction.

Frame event versus physical force

A “jump button pressed” event should not necessarily apply the same force every rendered frame while the button remains down. A one-shot impulse, a force over a defined simulation interval, and a controller velocity target are different game/physics contracts.

The same issue appears with explosions, springs and contact responses.

Fixed step

Simulation forces should normally be accumulated and integrated on the fixed simulation clock. Rendering interpolation does not apply physics again. If multiple rendering frames occur between physics ticks, repeating a force per render frame introduces frame-rate dependence.

Verification

Test the same physical scenario with different render rates but the same fixed simulation step. For impulses, verify momentum change directly. For forces, integrate over equal physical time and compare trajectories/convergence order.

Read the connected explanation in Continuous Notes/Game Engine - From First Frame to Living Worlds#From the push on a panel to a repeatable rigid-body simulator.

Related: Center of mass and inertia, Time integrators and symplectic updates.

Constraint-level continuation

Forces change momentum over time; collision impulses change momentum at a discrete event. tools/labs/constraint_friction_island_lab.cpp now connects that distinction to a minimal sequential-impulse solver: an approaching normal velocity produces a nonnegative impulse that removes approach, a tangential impulse is clamped by |jt|≤μjn|j_t|\le\mu j_n, and repeated sweeps propagate support through a two-body stack.

The same witness builds contact islands with union-find. This makes a practical ownership boundary visible: contacts couple bodies inside an island, while disconnected islands may be solved independently. Angular effective mass, restitution thresholds, warm starting, sleeping and a full two-dimensional friction cone remain higher solver layers.

DCC adapters and engine publication

DCC adapters and engine publication

A production pipeline should not let every DCC application define a different engine truth. Blender, Maya, Houdini and Nuke expose different object models, dependency systems and scripting APIs, but the engine-facing publication contract can remain host-neutral.

The useful separation is:

Host adapter → normalized asset description → validation → deterministic build plan → staged publication → engine-side verification.

The host adapter owns how to read the authoring application. The normalized core owns what the engine requires. Publication owns filesystem and identity guarantees. Engine verification proves that the published result can actually be consumed.

Blender boundary

Blender’s Python API exposes application data through the bpy module, including data access, context, operators, types, utilities and path helpers. A production exporter should prefer direct data access for deterministic inspection and use context-sensitive operators only when their context requirements are understood.

An adapter should establish which evaluated scene state it exports, how collections and object visibility are interpreted, which transforms are baked, and which external dependencies are copied or referenced. Exporting the editable authoring graph and exporting evaluated geometry are different contracts.

Primary reference: https://docs.blender.org/api/main/index.html

Maya boundary

Maya exposes both scripting commands and C++/Python APIs, with explicit dependency-graph and DAG plug-in concepts. A Maya adapter should distinguish scene hierarchy from dependency relationships and should make attribute/default/reference semantics explicit rather than flattening everything into names.

Primary reference: https://help.autodesk.com/view/MAYADEV/2026/ENU/

Houdini boundary

Houdini’s Object Model exposes nodes and geometry through the hou package. SOP networks generate geometry, while ROP networks can describe render/output dependencies. Geometry references can also depend on node cook state, so an adapter must decide when data is evaluated and copied into the host-neutral representation.

SideFX documentation explicitly distinguishes node families such as SOP geometry, LOP/USD scene description, ROP output networks and TOP task workflows. A pipeline should use those semantics instead of treating every node graph as the same kind of data.

Primary references: - https://www.sidefx.com/docs/houdini/hom/ - https://www.sidefx.com/docs/houdini/

Nuke boundary

Nuke publication often involves image nodes, knobs, file paths and frame ranges rather than mesh topology. The engine-neutral contract should therefore represent sequence ranges and missing-frame policy explicitly. Frame range syntax can represent contiguous and stepped ranges, so “first and last frame exist” is not sufficient validation.

Primary reference: https://learn.foundry.com/nuke/content/getting_started/managing_scripts/defining_frame_ranges.html

Host-neutral core

A normalized publication record should carry at least:

  • logical asset identity;
  • schema version;
  • source provenance;
  • normalized relative input/output paths;
  • declared coordinate/unit/color-space conventions where relevant;
  • dependencies;
  • content identity or cryptographic digest;
  • frame range or subresource inventory;
  • tool/version information when reproducibility depends on it;
  • deterministic diagnostics.

The core should not contain live bpy, Maya, hou or Nuke objects. Those are host-lifetime objects. Convert them into owned normalized data before asynchronous work or engine publication.

Validation before mutation

A dry-run plan should be complete before writing outputs. Validate path traversal, duplicate output destinations, missing dependencies, unsupported schema versions, frame gaps and identity collisions first.

Then write to staging locations. Only after every staged artifact passes validation should publication become visible. On filesystems where atomic replacement is relied upon, that property needs an actual platform/filesystem test; a logical transaction model does not prove disk semantics.

Executable witness

tools/labs/production_pipeline_contract_lab.cpp implements the host-neutral part of this design. It validates a portable relative-path grammar, rejects parent traversal, checks schema and SHA-256 string shape, produces a deterministic sorted publication plan, checks output collisions, models idempotent publication, and verifies contiguous frame sequences.

It deliberately does not claim real Blender/Maya/Houdini/Nuke execution, SHA-256 computation, symlink resolution, atomic rename behavior or render-farm integration.

Related: Atomic publication and durability, Binary format contracts, Interface contracts and publication.

Executed Blender boundary

The host-neutral adapter contract now has one real DCC execution path. tools/dcc/blender_contract.py runs inside Blender in background mode, creates mesh/collection/object datablocks without UI interaction, attaches logical publication metadata, saves a .blend, exports a binary glTF/GLB with extras, validates the GLB header/JSON chunk, resets Blender, re-imports the GLB and verifies mesh identity plus custom publication fields.

The GitHub workflow .github/workflows/blender-dcc-contract.yml installs Blender on Linux and executes that round trip headlessly. This changes the Blender portion from “API described” to “host executed in CI.” It does not upgrade Maya, Houdini or Nuke: their adapters remain host-neutral contracts until a licensed/current host can execute them. It also does not prove arbitrary production scenes, armatures, materials, texture packaging or current Kairo import parity.

Current Blender documentation explicitly supports background Python execution and glTF export; the repository test treats those host APIs as an external boundary and validates the exported artifact rather than assuming an operator call succeeded.

Production manifests and transactional publication

Production manifests and transactional publication

A production manifest is a durable description of what should be built and published. It prevents a pipeline from depending on hidden editor state or on “whatever files happen to be in this directory.”

A useful manifest separates identity from location. A logical asset ID names the thing the project means. Source and output paths say where a particular revision is read and written. A cryptographic digest can identify exact content bytes. A schema version says how to interpret all fields.

Path safety

Normalize paths before planning any write. A production-safe policy normally rejects parent traversal, unexpected absolute paths, ambiguous separators, and paths that escape the declared project root after symlink resolution.

Lexical normalization alone cannot prove symlink safety. The filesystem must be queried at the point where real paths are resolved, and the resolved target must still lie inside the approved root.

Deterministic plans

The same manifest and tool versions should produce the same ordered build plan. Determinism makes logs diffable, cache keys stable and failures reproducible.

Planning should be side-effect free. A dry run should reveal every intended output, overwrite, deletion and dependency before publication begins.

Staging and commit

A safe publication sequence is:

  1. validate the whole request;
  2. write derived outputs to staging names or directories;
  3. validate staged bytes and metadata;
  4. fsync or equivalent when durability is part of the promise;
  5. publish with the platform’s proven atomic replacement mechanism;
  6. update manifest/index state;
  7. retain enough evidence to diagnose rollback or partial failure.

Atomicity and durability are separate. A rename can make a new name appear atomically yet still not guarantee survival across power loss unless the required data and directory metadata were persisted.

Idempotence

Repeating the same publication should either be a no-op or produce the same visible state. A pipeline that appends duplicate records, increments versions accidentally or rewrites unrelated timestamps on every run is harder to cache and reason about.

tools/labs/production_pipeline_contract_lab.cpp models deterministic plan generation and idempotent publication in memory. It intentionally labels real filesystem durability as unproved.

Related: Atomic publication and durability, DCC adapters and engine publication.

Interface contracts and publication

Interface contracts and publication

An interface contract says more than which function name to call. It defines the states in which an operation is valid and what becomes true when it succeeds.

A complete contract should state:

  • valid input domain and units;
  • ownership and lifetime of arguments/results;
  • mutation and aliasing;
  • failure representation and exception/error guarantees;
  • thread/concurrency rules;
  • timing: immediate, deferred or asynchronous;
  • invalidation;
  • observability/publication point.

Publication is a state transition

A producer may construct a resource privately and then publish it so consumers can rely on it. Before publication, partial state can remain invisible. After publication, every documented invariant must hold.

For CPU concurrency, release/acquire synchronization is one possible publication mechanism when the memory model requirements fit the data structure.

For asynchronous assets, “decode finished” does not mean “GPU resource is safe to sample.” A useful state machine may distinguish:

requested → decoded → upload recorded → submitted → GPU-ready → published.

Similarly, an obsolete request must not publish after a newer generation has replaced it. Generation IDs or request tokens protect the destination identity.

Ownership versus readiness

A reference can be alive but not ready. A GPU buffer wrapper can exist while its upload is still in flight. Conversely, a resource can be GPU-ready while the CPU owner is about to destroy it unless retirement is deferred until all GPU use completes.

Lifetime and synchronization are independent axes.

Failure guarantees

If publication is atomic, consumers should observe either the old valid version or the new valid version, not a half-updated mixture. That promise requires implementation evidence appropriate to the domain: atomics/locks for CPU state, transaction/staging for files, semaphore/fence/queue dependencies for GPU work.

Evidence

tools/labs/threaded_asset_publication_lab.cpp and tools/labs/production_pipeline_contract_lab.cpp exercise two different publication domains: concurrent asset decoding/publication and deterministic staged production publication.

Read the connected explanation in Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs#An API is a promise about an operation.

Related: Atomic publication and durability, Production manifests and transactional publication, Vulkan synchronization2 and resource transitions.

End-to-end disk event stepping and randomized supervision — November 12, 2026

An additional stand-alone C++20 laboratory at tools/labs/disk_event_pipeline_lab.cpp now connects continuous disk collision discovery to a complete fixed-duration state update. It repeatedly finds the earliest encounter among all unordered disk pairs, advances all positions to the event, groups approximately simultaneous events, freezes each incoming restitution target, runs 32 accumulated projected normal-impulse sweeps, and re-queries the remaining interval. Nine fixed scenes exercise collision timing against a static body, two-body elastic energy/momentum, symmetric simultaneous contacts, separating motion, initial overlap rejection, event budget failure, chained events, ideal inelastic response, and duplicate stable-ID / zero-duration validation.

Discovered defect and correction: the first nine scenes passed, but a separately constructed deterministic 10,000-case unequal-mass isolated-pair experiment failed at trial 937. A valid impact had advanced two centres to a near-tangent configuration whose squared distance was a tiny amount below the squared combined radius; the original squared-distance tolerance rejected it as a deep overlap. The published correction computes the linear centre gap and uses a finite-precision length tolerance scaled to world-coordinate magnitude. After this correction, all 10,000 seeded cases passed under GCC and Clang and sanitizer tests. No claim is made that this tolerance is globally robust for arbitrary very large/very small coordinate ratios.

The successful randomized experiment has been retained as independently executable tools/labs/disk_event_property_lab.cpp. For each isolated impact it checks exactly one event, Newton’s restitution equation, linear momentum conservation and non-increasing kinetic energy. Both newly published source files were re-fetched from GitHub and their Git blob hashes matched the locally compiled files: event pipeline e69b18ba580329db14ef0bde18811e6737790084 and property test caa2fffdfe32048e6580887ad868eda36278700f. Local strict C++20 GCC/Clang builds and combined AddressSanitizer/UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer executions passed. The shared workflow is configured to run both on GitHub but its hosted execution has not yet been confirmed. The contact narrative and README now link both sources and explain the numeric trace.

Remaining boundary: this is not a production Kairo world step; all-pairs event search is quadratic per rescan, contact detection is constant-velocity disk-only, friction/rotation and resting contacts are excluded, and thrown exceptions can leave the scene partially advanced. Fully robust CCD predicates, broadphase acceleration, transactional state restoration, general convex shapes, long-time stacks, numerical determinism under compiler/platform changes and runtime integration remain open. No prior video/book claim-review queue counts were incremented by this engineering experiment.

Swept broad-phase candidate oracle and conservation check — November 12, 2026

The repository now contains tools/labs/swept_broadphase_lab.cpp, a tested reference implementation of constant-velocity disk swept-AABB candidate filtering. It conservatively constructs outward-rounded bounds, sorts by minimum x, tracks active x intervals and tests y overlap, then produces unique sorted candidate pairs. Each exact disk collision returned by a separately implemented analytic TOI oracle must be included in those candidates. The test covers a crossing scene, a 100-disk non-interacting scene, 200 seeded randomized 35-disk scenes, duplicate IDs and negative dt. The randomized comparison examines 200 × (35 × 34 / 2) = 119,000 possible pairs for missed collisions. GCC and Clang strict C++20 builds and a local combined AddressSanitizer/UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer build passed, and the GitHub source Git-blob SHA 11f9e86dbf1ee850e64b5dafdea63427b2177187 matched the compiled local source. The CI workflow includes this new lab but no GitHub-hosted run was confirmed here.

The broadphase is not integrated into the disk event stepper; it therefore establishes a conservative candidate-generation proof obligation in a small witness, not measured engine acceleration. The simple vector active set can still take O(n²) time in dense scenes, and floating-point accuracy, rapidly changing acceleration, general shapes, real scene data and production determinism remain unverified. Incremental contact penetration refresh

Incremental contact penetration refresh

Position correction moves every contact point attached to the corrected bodies. For a small rotation, its first-order point displacement is translation plus rotation vector crossed with the pre-correction world-space lever arm. Project the difference of the two point movements onto the frozen contact normal, using the declared normal and penetration signs.

Refresh each known contact once for the correction just applied, then reconsider the worst penetration. Reusing an old correction counts movement twice. This local estimate cannot discover new contacts or replace geometry refresh after substantial rotation or a feature change.

Spring forces and numerical integration

Spring forces and numerical integration

For displacement from an endpoint to a particle, the ideal spring force preserves the sign of extension: stretching pulls toward the endpoint; compression pushes away. A bungee has zero force while slack and pulls only when stretched. Coincident endpoints need an explicit direction policy. Force magnitude alone cannot detect a direction error.

The force law and the time integrator are separate contracts. An undamped oscillator grows under forward Euler at every positive step size; semi-implicit Euler has a different bounded interval. An analytic target position does not become a reachable current-step position merely by converting it to force. Physical stiffness, mass-normalized coefficients and numerical damping settings need distinct units and definitions.

Partial derivatives and gradients

Partial derivatives and gradients

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9

Definition and mechanism

For a function of several inputs, a partial derivative varies one coordinate while holding the others fixed. Collecting these derivatives gives the gradient for a scalar-valued function. The gradient is a covector of first-order sensitivities: its pairing with a small displacement predicts the scalar change. Under the Euclidean inner product, the gradient vector points in the direction of steepest ascent, and its negative gives steepest local descent. Coordinate scaling changes derivative magnitudes and can therefore change optimization behavior. A partial derivative is not generally the full effect when inputs move together; that requires the total derivative or directional derivative. In graphics, gradients describe image sensitivity to geometry or material parameters, while their coordinates must be interpreted with the parameter units and basis used by the model.

Ray-triangle intersection

Ray-triangle intersection

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

A ray is a parametric half-line r(t)=o+tdr(t)=o+td, where oo is its origin, dd is its direction, and only t≥0t\ge0 lies ahead of the ray. To intersect a triangle, first intersect the ray with its plane, then express the hit point in barycentric coordinates and accept it only if the weights lie inside the triangle. An equivalent determinant test solves for ray distance and two barycentric coordinates together. The hit record should state whether the result is nearest, any, or all intersections; those are different query contracts. Parallel or nearly parallel rays, degenerate triangles, and hits near edges require care because small floating-point errors can change classification. Scale-aware tolerances and consistent orientation predicates reduce cracks and self-intersection artifacts.

Camera calibration and bundle adjustment

Camera calibration and bundle adjustment

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

Camera calibration estimates parameters that map 3D points to image coordinates. Intrinsics describe focal scale, principal point, and lens distortion; extrinsics describe camera pose relative to the scene. Known calibration targets provide 3D-to-2D correspondences, and a nonlinear least-squares objective minimizes reprojection error. Bundle adjustment jointly refines many camera poses and 3D feature points by minimizing all observed image residuals. The problem is sparse because each image sees only a subset of points. It also has gauge freedoms: translating or scaling the entire reconstruction may leave projections unchanged, so fix a reference pose or scale. Robust loss functions reduce the effect of mismatched features. Good initialization, parameter scaling, and Jacobian structure determine whether optimization converges.

Homogeneous clipping and perspective interpolation

Homogeneous clipping and perspective interpolation

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

After a vertex is transformed, its clip-space coordinate is (xc,yc,zc,wc)(x_c,y_c,z_c,w_c). Clip primitives against the view volume before perspective division; under the conventional OpenGL clip convention the inequalities are −wc≤xc,yc,zc≤wc-w_c\le x_c,y_c,z_c\le w_c. A crossing edge is split by interpolating its homogeneous endpoints, which preserves the projective line and avoids dividing by a small or negative ww too early. Only surviving points are divided by wcw_c to enter normalized device coordinates. Attributes then need perspective-correct interpolation: screen-space barycentric weights interpolate a/wa/w and 1/w1/w, and the fragment value is their ratio. For a triangle with weights λi\lambda_i, a=(∑iλiai/wi)/(∑iλi/wi)a=(\sum_i\lambda_i a_i/w_i)/(\sum_i\lambda_i/w_i). Direct linear interpolation in screen space is correct only for affine quantities or equal depth; otherwise textures warp. Clip-space depth conventions and the near/far interval vary by API and projection setup, so the inequalities must match the active pipeline.

Phase 11 camera development

Clipping and perspective-correct interpolation preserve projective geometry, while texture filtering asks how much surface area maps to a pixel. Neighboring camera rays approximate the image-to-surface footprint. At grazing angles one pixel can cover a long, thin region; a center-only texel lookup may alias detail even when attributes interpolate correctly. Use footprint estimates to select mip levels or anisotropic filters, while respecting visibility edges where derivatives jump. Ray differentials aid sampling but do not replace clipping or multisample coverage. Source basis: PBRT differential-ray texture filtering. Executable raster-state continuation

The project now carries two complementary CPU witnesses. tools/labs/raster_reference_lab.cpp owns edge coverage, barycentrics, perspective-correct interpolation and depth ordering. tools/labs/raster_pipeline_state_lab.cpp continues the same pipeline through a homogeneous clip-plane intersection, an explicit four-sample coverage mask, stencil compare/pass update and premultiplied source-over blending.

That separation is deliberate: clipping happens in homogeneous coordinates before divide-by-ww; sample ownership happens after screen mapping; stencil/depth are stateful per-fragment/sample decisions; blending combines a surviving source with an existing destination. Treating all of them as “rasterization” without preserving these boundaries makes debugging nearly impossible.

Position reconstruction from depth

Position reconstruction from depth

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 11 · Latest development: Phase 11

Definition and mechanism

Given a pixel and an axial depth value, reconstruct a view-space point by converting the pixel to NDC, forming its camera ray, and scaling that ray so its forward-axis component equals the measured depth. Alternatively, transform the corresponding homogeneous clip point through an inverse projection matrix and divide by its resulting homogeneous coordinate. To obtain world position, apply the inverse view transform. These routes must share the actual viewport, pixel-centre, NDC-depth, and projection conventions used to render the image. In large worlds, subtract camera-relative origins before reducing precision; converting an already-rounded coordinate cannot restore lost detail. In a camera-relative renderer, reconstruct near the camera origin before adding a large global offset.

Camera gauge freedoms and observability

Camera gauge freedoms and observability

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 11

Definition and mechanism

A gauge freedom is a coordinated change to unknown scene and camera parameters that leaves every measured image unchanged. In calibrated monocular structure from motion, translating and rotating the entire reconstruction changes only the chosen world frame, while a common scale change of points and camera translations preserves projections; absolute metric scale therefore needs an external reference. Observability asks which local parameter changes produce distinguishable measurements. Linearizing reprojection residuals gives a Jacobian; its weighted information tensor or matrix J𝖳WJJ^{\mathsf T}WJ reveals weak parameter combinations through small eigenvalues after gauge directions are fixed. Example: adding more points to one planar, nearly fronto-parallel view may reduce pixel noise while focal length and distance remain strongly coupled. These conclusions assume a stated camera/scene model, correctly associated observations, and local linearization; the information matrix diagnoses local constraints, not global uniqueness. Report uncertainty only after fixing the gauge and specifying the observation noise model.

Example: A monocular map can be uniformly enlarged with all camera translations enlarged by the same factor and render the same images; a known baseline or measured object length fixes that scale gauge.

Assumptions: The gauge statement assumes calibrated monocular perspective cameras and no metric prior.; The information-matrix interpretation is local and depends on residual weighting and parameterization.

QR factorization and least squares

QR factorization and least squares

QR writes A=QRA=QR with orthonormal columns in QQ and triangular RR. Orthogonal coordinates preserve Euclidean lengths, so least squares reduces to a triangular solve and a perpendicular residual. Householder QR is a stable dense method; Gram–Schmidt explains the geometry but can lose orthogonality.

Use it when: fitting overdetermined data with known full column rank.

Developed in Phase 8: Orthogonal transformations change coordinates without changing Euclidean lengths. QR therefore separates the fitted component, solved through triangular RR, from the constant perpendicular residual; the Householder construction is the stable dense route, with Gram–Schmidt retained to make the geometry visible. Singular value decomposition

Singular value decomposition

For any real rectangular matrix, A=UΣV𝖳A=U\Sigma V^\mathsf T. Right singular vectors are input directions, left singular vectors are output directions, and nonnegative singular values are principal stretches. Unlike eigenvectors, the two sets live in different spaces.

Use it when: revealing rank and conditioning, solving rank-uncertain least squares, compressing a matrix, or understanding PCA.

Developed in Phase 8: The SVD expresses a rectangular map using orthonormal input and output directions joined by nonnegative stretches. Full, thin, and compact shapes have different dimensions; bidiagonal reduction and Jacobi methods compute the factors, and reconstruction, orthogonality, and triplet residuals check them independently. factor shapes · SVD algorithms and validation

Used by

University course development

Extend the existing factorization note with its role in estimation, conditioning, and geometry. For matrix AA, the decomposition A=UΣVTA=U\Sigma V^T separates orthogonal input directions, axis-aligned scaling, and orthogonal output directions. Singular values on the diagonal of Σ\Sigma quantify how strongly each independent direction is preserved; a zero or tiny value signals rank loss or poor conditioning. Least-squares fitting can use this structure to identify which parameter combinations are well constrained and to avoid amplifying measurement noise along nearly invisible directions. The same analysis explains why a camera calibration or bundle-adjustment system can have gauge freedoms: translating or scaling the entire reconstruction may leave image measurements unchanged. Singular values diagnose these ambiguities, while constraints or fixed reference poses remove them. Thus SVD links linear algebra to robust vision, not just matrix compression.

Depth buffering and visibility order

Depth buffering and visibility order

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

A depth buffer stores the nearest depth seen so far for each image sample. When rasterizing a fragment, compare its depth with the stored value; if it is closer, update both depth and color, otherwise discard it. This per-sample test resolves opaque visibility without sorting all triangles. Perspective projection maps view-space depth nonlinearly, so the near and far clipping planes affect how floating-point precision is distributed. If they span an unnecessarily huge ratio, nearly coplanar surfaces may quantize to equal or inconsistent depths and flicker as the camera moves; this is z-fighting. Alpha-blended surfaces need additional ordering or order-independent methods because color composition is not commutative. Depth establishes visibility, while transparency determines how multiple visible layers contribute.

Prerequisites

  • Camera view and clip-space pipeline

Reversed-Z and nonlinear perspective depth require consistent reconstruction before threshold comparisons. Valid visibility does not guarantee photometric stability after lighting, exposure, or material changes. Link depth semantics to temporal history validation. Lens optics and depth of field

Lens optics and depth of field

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

A pinhole camera maps every scene point to one image point through a single center, but a real lens has a finite aperture. Rays from one object point pass through different parts of the aperture and meet at a focused image point only for the chosen focus distance. Points nearer or farther from that plane form a blur disk called the circle of confusion. Stopping down the aperture narrows the cone of rays and increases depth of field, but reduces collected light and may require longer exposure or higher sensor gain. Focal length and focus distance also affect field of view and perspective magnification. A thin-lens model is an approximation; real lenses add aberrations and vignetting. The model helps explain why depth of field is both an optical effect and a sampling/integration process over aperture positions.

Prerequisites

Phase 11 camera development

A pinhole camera emits one ideal ray per image location. A finite-aperture lens samples a family of rays whose intersections form a blur disk away from the focal plane. A thin-lens camera therefore samples film and lens position, then aims through a focal point. Differentials from film offsets alone omit aperture variation unless the model includes it. Monte Carlo PDFs and camera weights must match the sampled film/aperture measure. The thin-lens model approximates real optics; aberrations and bokeh shape require richer models. GPU vertex specification

GPU vertex specification

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

A GPU vertex-input specification explains how bytes in one or more buffers become per-vertex shader inputs. A buffer object owns bytes; a vertex array object records their interpretation: enabled attributes, component count and type, normalization, stride, byte offset, and the buffer binding used for fetch. Stride is the number of bytes between successive vertices; offset is the first component’s byte position. For vertex i, the address is base + offset + i × stride. For interleaved records containing position (3 floats), normal (3), and UV (2), the stride is 8 × 4 = 32 bytes and the UV offset is 24 bytes. Modern binding APIs separate attribute format from the buffer binding; older pointer-style calls can capture the buffer bound at setup time. A wrong stride may still address valid memory, so the symptom is often plausible but scrambled geometry. The contract must agree with CPU packing, shader input types, and the API’s state-capture rules.

Axial depth and Euclidean range

Axial depth and Euclidean range

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 11 · Latest development: Phase 11

Definition and mechanism

Axial depth measures distance along the camera’s forward axis; Euclidean range measures distance from the camera centre along the viewing ray. With a right-handed view frame looking along −Z-Z, positive axial depth is d=−zd=-z, while range is r=x2+y2+z2r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}. They agree only on the optical axis. For a unit ray direction qq with qz<0q_z<0, a range measurement converts to axial depth as d=−rqzd=-rq_z. A range sensor and a perspective depth buffer may therefore encode different quantities. Applying a depth-buffer formula directly to a range image distorts reconstructed geometry away from the image centre. At view point (3,4,−12)(3,4,-12), axial depth is 1212 while range is 1313, a visible distinction off-axis.

Ray differentials and camera sampling measures

Ray differentials and camera sampling measures

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 11

Definition and mechanism

A camera sample selects a film location and usually a shutter time, then maps that sample to a weighted ray or path contribution. Ray differentials approximate how neighboring pixel samples change the generated ray; after intersection they estimate the surface footprint covered by a pixel and help choose a texture filter level. A sampling measure states which quantity is sampled and therefore which probability density belongs in a Monte Carlo estimator; area, solid angle, image-plane area, and discrete pixel measures are not interchangeable without a Jacobian. Example: two adjacent pixels generate rays whose intersection points span a large patch on a distant oblique surface, so filtering should average that footprint rather than use a single high-frequency texel. Differential rays are local first-order approximations and can fail at discontinuities or complex lens mappings; the weight and PDF must match the camera model and chosen measure.

Example: For a pinhole camera, offset the raster sample by one pixel in x and y, generate neighboring rays, and intersect them with a textured plane; the resulting parallelogram estimates the pixel footprint for texture filtering.

Assumptions: Differentials approximate nearby rays locally and are not exact at visibility or lens discontinuities.; Importance weights/PDFs are valid only when defined in the same measure as the estimator.

RAII and resource handles

RAII and resource handles

Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C010 · Latest development: C010

Definition and mechanism

Resource Acquisition Is Initialization (RAII) ties a cleanup responsibility to a well-defined object’s lifetime. A resource handle acquires or adopts responsibility, preserves the release protocol through moves/composition, and performs matching cleanup on scope exit—including ordinary exception unwinding. The resource can be a memory allocation, lock, file, socket, native GPU object, or other paired protocol. RAII does not itself prove that an external asynchronous user has finished; it must trigger the correct deferred-release protocol.

Construction failure cleans completed subobjects, so each acquired responsibility should enter an owner immediately. A raw native handle is not an owner unless its release contract is implemented and documented.

Prerequisites

  • Storage duration and object lifetime — Object scope and resource lifetime must be distinguished.
  • Destruction and partial construction — Completed owner subobjects clean up during failure.

Used by

  • Exclusive and shared smart-pointer ownership
  • Placement construction and explicit lifetime management

Exclusive and shared smart-pointer ownership

Exclusive and shared smart-pointer ownership

Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C010 · Latest development: C010

Definition and mechanism

std::unique_ptr<T, D> is a move-only exclusive owner whose deleter D defines disposal. get() exposes a borrow; release() transfers the responsibility without deleting. std::shared_ptr<T> joins a shared ownership group represented by a control block; the managed object is destroyed when the last strong owner is released. The control block can outlive the object while weak observers remain. The stored pointer and the object whose destruction the control block arranges can differ (for example, aliasing ownership).

Shared ownership is not pointee synchronization. Concurrent operations on distinct smart-pointer handles do not automatically make concurrent access to T safe. Use sharing only when several independent parties truly retain the same lifetime.

Prerequisites

  • Ownership and non-owning views — Access-only views and ownership responsibilities are different contracts.
  • RAII and resource handles — Smart pointers are standard resource owners built around lifetime-bound cleanup.

Used by

Storage duration and object lifetime

Storage duration and object lifetime

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C003 · Latest development: C010

Definition and mechanism

Direct local reference binding can extend a temporary under specified rules; a returned parameter alias does not renew the deadline. A reference’s own lifetime does not prove the referent’s lifetime.

Construction and destruction can delimit an occupant while backing storage remains. The inline C++ lab uses construct_at/destroy_at in an alignas byte buffer and new/delete as the combined allocation/construction and destruction/release operations. The pointer object does not own or extend pointee life. Implicit object creation occurs only for specified operations and suitable types; a reinterpret_cast is not a universal construction operation.

Storage duration specifies how long storage is potentially available: automatic, static, thread, or dynamic. Object lifetime describes when a particular initialized object exists within it. Old bytes can remain after lifetime ends without authorizing access. const restricts mutation, not physical placement. Language categories do not dictate a universal segment map.

M010 reuses this separation for smart owners and arenas: a wrapper’s storage duration, the managed object’s lifetime, the ownership-group lifetime, and an external GPU-use interval may all end at different times. Placement construction reuses suitable live storage; object destruction alone does not return that storage to an allocator.

Prerequisites

  • Interpretation contract — Representation, type, and lifetime must identify what object exists.

Executed POSIX durability sequence

The durability contract now has an actual syscall-level witness in tools/labs/atomic_publication_durability_lab.cpp.

The reference creates a staging file with exclusive creation, writes the complete payload, calls fsync on the file, closes it, renames it within the same directory, opens the containing directory, and calls fsync on that directory before treating publication as complete. It then verifies the final bytes and absence of the staging name. Separate tests reject a pre-existing staging file and a traversal-style final name.

This is stronger than “write temp then rename,” because rename atomicity and durable persistence are different properties. The file sync requests persistence of file contents/metadata; the directory sync requests persistence of the directory-entry change. Successful calls on CI are evidence that the operating-system/filesystem accepted that ordering. They are not a laboratory power-cut test and cannot promise identical persistence guarantees on every filesystem, storage controller, Windows API, network filesystem or production asset pipeline.

Prefix scan and stream compaction

Prefix scan and stream compaction

A prefix scan turns local counts into globally consistent offsets. For an exclusive sum scan of input xx,

y0=0,yi=∑j=0i−1xj. y_0=0, \qquad y_i=\sum_{j=0}^{i-1}x_j.

If each element says how many output records it will emit, yiy_i is the first output slot owned by element ii. This converts a race-prone global append into deterministic non-overlapping regions.

For Boolean compaction, let predicate bi∈{0,1}b_i\in\{0,1\}. Scan bb to obtain offsets. Every active element with bi=1b_i=1 writes itself to output[scan[i]]. The final output count is scan[n-1] + b[n-1].

Parallel structure

The naive parallel scan that repeatedly doubles an offset performs O(nlog⁡n)O(n\log n) work. A work-efficient tree scan performs an up-sweep/reduction followed by a down-sweep and uses O(n)O(n) work with O(log⁡n)O(\log n) depth.

On a GPU, a practical large-array scan normally has several levels:

  1. scan each workgroup block into local output;
  2. record each block total;
  3. scan the block totals;
  4. add each scanned block offset back into that block’s local results.

Every phase has a dependency. Dispatching all phases without establishing visibility/order is not a valid scan merely because each shader is individually correct.

Shared-memory bank conflicts and subgroup width affect performance, while workgroup barriers only synchronize participating invocations in that workgroup.

Stream compaction as an allocation proof

Compaction is useful beyond filtering visible objects. It appears in GPU-driven draw generation, BVH construction, particle survival, tiled light lists, Gaussian tile duplication and sparse work queues.

The scan proves that each surviving producer owns a distinct range before any scatter writes occur.

Evidence boundary

The current repository has CPU-side scan/compaction reasoning in the canonical volumes but does not yet claim a native Vulkan/Metal scan kernel benchmark. The next hardware proof should compare a scalar CPU oracle, a workgroup implementation, multi-workgroup hierarchy, adversarial non-power-of-two sizes, and captured GPU timing.

Primary background: NVIDIA GPU Gems 3, Chapter 39, “Parallel Prefix Sum (Scan) with CUDA.”

Teach and reconstruct: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs#Scan turns local counts into nonoverlapping output regions.

Related: GPU workgroups and synchronization, BVH build traversal and workload selection.

Manifold polygon meshes and boundary structure

Manifold polygon meshes and boundary structure

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

A polygon mesh is a combinatorial surface made of vertices, edges, and faces plus an embedding that assigns each vertex a position. Manifoldness is a local connectivity condition: an interior edge belongs to two faces, and the faces around each interior vertex form one cycle or fan. At a boundary, an edge belongs to one face and the vertex neighborhood forms one open chain; each boundary component closes into a loop. A bow-tie vertex with two disconnected fans is nonmanifold even if every face is an ordinary triangle. These conditions let algorithms define an unambiguous local tangent neighborhood, traversal, and surface orientation. Connectivity validity does not guarantee good geometry: valid topology can still self-intersect, collapse to a point, or contain poor skinny triangles. Keep topological and geometric quality checks separate.

Radiance fields and Gaussian splatting

Radiance fields and Gaussian splatting

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

A radiance field represents a scene by the color and density seen along each 3D viewing ray. NeRF maps a position and viewing direction through a learned function, then volume-renders samples using transmittance and opacity weights; multiple calibrated photographs supervise the result. This representation handles view-dependent appearance but can require many ray samples and careful camera alignment. 3D Gaussian splatting instead stores anisotropic colored Gaussian primitives in space and projects them to screen, sorting and blending their footprints for fast interactive views. 2D Gaussian splatting uses oriented surface-like splats to improve geometric consistency. These methods trade continuous function evaluation for explicit primitives and rasterization. Sparse or biased views leave unseen regions unconstrained; floaters, blur, aliasing, incorrect transparency ordering, or poor geometry can remain even when training views look convincing. Novel-view quality is not equivalent to a watertight mesh or physically correct material. Reconstruction quality depends on camera poses, coverage, calibration, and the scene’s changing illumination.

  • Sampling aliasing and reconstruction
  • Probability density and change of measure
  • Bounding volume hierarchies
  • Ray-triangle intersection
  • Automatic differentiation and backpropagation
  • Latent-variable models and generative flows

Time integrators and symplectic updates

Time integrators and symplectic updates

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9

Definition and mechanism

A time integrator turns a differential equation into a discrete state update. Explicit Euler uses the current slope; midpoint and Runge–Kutta methods combine several slope evaluations to improve local accuracy; semi-implicit Euler updates velocity before position and can behave better for mechanical systems. Symplectic methods preserve the geometric structure of Hamiltonian dynamics, often keeping long-run energy error bounded rather than allowing systematic drift. No method is universally best: order, stability region, cost, conservation, and stiffness all matter. A higher formal order does not guarantee better behavior at an unsuitable step size or under discontinuous forces. Compare integrators on the same problem, step policy, and error target. Update order is part of the algorithm: changing it can change stability and physical behavior, not merely code style.

Prerequisites

  • ODE initial-value problems and stiffness

  • ODE integration and stability

Vulkan synchronization2 and resource transitions

Vulkan synchronization2 and resource transitions

Vulkan synchronization is not “put a barrier between two passes.” A dependency has to connect a real producer access to a real consumer access with execution and memory scopes that cover both operations.

Vulkan 1.3 includes the synchronization2 model promoted from VK_KHR_synchronization2. It places stage and access masks together in the version-2 barrier structures and uses commands such as vkCmdPipelineBarrier2 and vkQueueSubmit2.

Primary references: - https://docs.vulkan.org/guide/latest/extensions/VK_KHR_synchronization2.html - https://docs.vulkan.org/spec/latest/chapters/synchronization.html

Producer → consumer reasoning

For every hazard, write the transition in words first.

Example:

A transfer command writes a storage buffer. A later compute shader reads that buffer.

The producer execution stage is transfer. The producer access is transfer write. The consumer execution stage is compute shader. The consumer access is shader storage read.

An abstract memory barrier therefore needs to cover:

source stage = TRANSFER
source access = TRANSFER_WRITE
destination stage = COMPUTE_SHADER
destination access = SHADER_STORAGE_READ.

Using ALL_COMMANDS and MEMORY_READ/WRITE everywhere may accidentally work but destroys precision and can hide misunderstanding. Using a destination stage that never performs the consumer access is not made correct by a broad access mask.

Image transitions add a layout contract

Images have another state dimension: layout. An image memory barrier can both synchronize accesses and transition from oldLayout to newLayout. The old layout must describe the state established by prior use unless the contents are intentionally discarded under the rules that permit that.

A render graph therefore needs more than “read” and “write.” For each image subresource it eventually needs:

  • stage/access usage;
  • required layout;
  • aspect;
  • mip range;
  • array-layer range;
  • queue ownership when queues/families differ.

A whole-image state tracker is a valid early implementation but cannot claim correct independent mip/layer scheduling.

Queue submission and timeline semaphores

Synchronization2 also modernizes queue submission through VkSubmitInfo2 and related structures. Timeline semaphores carry monotonically increasing integer values and are useful for expressing ordered completion points across submissions. A timeline value is not a memory barrier by itself; the signal/wait operations participate in dependencies whose scopes must still match the work.

Native witness now in the repository

tools/native/vulkan_sync_smoke.cpp is compiled and executed in the dedicated native graphics workflow on Ubuntu with a Vulkan implementation and validation layer packages. It:

  • creates a Vulkan 1.3 instance;
  • finds a device exposing synchronization2;
  • creates a queue/device with the feature enabled;
  • records a VkMemoryBarrier2 through vkCmdPipelineBarrier2;
  • submits the command buffer using vkQueueSubmit2;
  • waits for fence completion;
  • fails on validation-layer errors when the layer is available.

That materially raises the evidence level from a CPU-only logical graph.

It still does not prove a resource-specific RAW transition, image layout transition, queue-family transfer, timeline protocol, transient aliasing, physical-GPU performance, or current Kairo/Vulkax integration. Each of those needs its own captured witness.

Related: GPU workgroups and synchronization, Rendering history validity, Render graph barrier lowering.
