Rigid Contact - Persistent Manifolds and Solver Reconstruction

Rigid contacts: from point velocity to a persistent contact manifold

Scope: original, independently reconstructed teaching for the existing engine collision-response narrative. The executable witnesses are rigid_contact_lab.cpp and persistent_contact_lab.cpp. These are 2D velocity-level CPU witnesses; they do not claim to be Kairo’s engine implementation, 3D production manifold generation, or continuous collision detection. Symbols and sign conventions below follow those two witnesses.

Why a contact is a constraint rather than a force chosen by eye

Imagine a box descending onto a static floor. The collision detector reports that the geometry is touching or overlapping, but it does not say which velocities are physically admissible. With body A as the floor and body B as the box, define the contact normal n to point from A toward B. At contact position p, the lever arms measured from each body’s centre of mass are r_A = p − x_A and r_B = p − x_B. For a planar rigid body, its point velocity is v(p) = v_com + ω × r, where planar scalar angular speed ω produces ω × (r_x,r_y) = (−ω r_y, ω r_x). This matters because an object rotating toward the floor can be closing at a corner even when the centre of mass is moving away.

The relative velocity of the two material points is u = (v_B + ω_B × r_B) − (v_A + ω_A × r_A). The normal component u_n = u · n tells us whether those two points are closing (u_n < 0) or separating (u_n > 0). For a non-penetrating unilateral contact without restitution, the desired post-solve condition is u_n ≥ 0, with a nonnegative accumulated contact impulse λ_n ≥ 0. Their complementarity condition is λ_n u_n = 0 at an exact solution: either the contact carries a positive separating-prevention impulse and reaches zero normal speed, or the bodies separate freely and the contact carries no impulse. Finite-iteration solvers only approximate this coupled condition.

Deriving effective inverse mass, rather than memorizing its denominator

The impulse on B is +λ n and the reaction on A is −λ n. Newton’s linear momentum law gives Δv_B = +λ m_B⁻¹ n and Δv_A = −λ m_A⁻¹ n. Angular impulse about the centre of mass gives Δω_B = +λ I_B⁻¹ (r_B × n) and Δω_A = −λ I_A⁻¹ (r_A × n), where the planar cross product of vectors is the scalar r_x n_y − r_y n_x. A rotation changes point velocity through Δω × r, and its projection onto n adds an angular term proportional to the squared lever arm.

Consequently the normal relative velocity changes by Δu_n = k_n λ, where

kn=mA−1+mB−1+IA−1(rA×n)2+IB−1(rB×n)2. k_n = m_A^{-1} + m_B^{-1} + I_A^{-1}(r_A \times n)^2 + I_B^{-1}(r_B \times n)^2.

Here k_n is inverse effective mass in the contact direction, not mass itself. The same physical impulse changes normal speed less when the effective mass is large. The equation follows from the full point-velocity update; it is not valid to omit rotational terms whenever the contact is off-centre. A static body uses zero inverse mass and inertia, but two completely unresponsive bodies yield k_n = 0 and must not be divided by. The corresponding tangential value k_t is obtained by substituting the perpendicular unit tangent t = (−n_y, n_x) for n.

For a desired post-impact normal speed b, one unconstrained correction is Δλ = (b − u_n)/k_n. A real contact cannot pull the bodies together, so the accumulated normal multiplier is projected:

λnnew=max⁡(0,λnold+b−unkn). \lambda_n^{new}=\max\left(0,\lambda_n^{old} + \frac{b-u_n}{k_n}\right).

Apply only the difference, Δλ_n = λ_n^{new} − λ_n^{old}, to body velocities. Applying the whole accumulated value every iteration would add the same historical impulse repeatedly, making motion energy grow artificially. Conversely, resetting the accumulator on every sweep defeats the projected Gauss–Seidel interpretation and prevents reliable friction bounds.

Restitution is a contact-creation decision, not a new bounce each iteration

For an impact with pre-solve normal speed u_n^before < −v_threshold, the outgoing speed target in this simplified solver is b = −e u_n^before, with restitution coefficient e ∈ [0,1]. This target must be sampled before contact impulses change the velocity and then held fixed during the iteration. If a solver recomputes b from the current velocity at every visit, a persistent resting point can acquire artificial new bounce energy. The witness distinguishes a new impact from a persistent contact through an explicit newImpact argument; a production engine requires an actual contact-state machine and impact detection so the decision is not left to a careless caller.

For the central collision test, both bodies have mass 1 kg, A starts at 2 m/s, B at 0 m/s, and the normal is +x. Their relative closing speed is −2 m/s; with e=1 and k_n=2 kg⁻¹, we need Δλ_n = (2 − (−2))/2 = 2 kg·m/s. The resulting velocities are 0 m/s and 2 m/s. Linear momentum remains 2 kg·m/s, and the kinetic energy remains 2 joules. This equality is specific to the elastic, frictionless, central, idealized two-body case—not a conservation promise for frictional or inelastic impacts.

Why friction depends on the normal impulse

For the upward normal n=(0,1) the laboratory chooses the tangent t=(−1,0). The sliding box initially moves at +3 m/s in x, so its tangent-coordinate velocity is u_t = −3 m/s. The unconstrained tangent impulse is −u_t/k_t; here k_t=1 kg⁻¹, giving +3 kg·m/s. The normal collision supplies λ_n=2 kg·m/s. With coefficient μ=0.5, the Coulomb limit is μλ_n=1 kg·m/s, so the stored tangent impulse is +1, not −1. Multiplying +1 × (−1,0) produces an x-directed impulse of (−1,0), reducing the box’s x velocity from +3 to +2 m/s. The sign of the stored scalar is relative to the chosen tangent direction; it cannot be interpreted without that basis.

The projected update is λ_t^{new} = clamp(λ_t^{old} − u_t/k_t, −μλ_n, +μλ_n). This is a scalar tangent model for 2D; real 3D contact has a two-dimensional tangent plane and requires a disk-cone constraint or a chosen approximation. The witness applies a single coefficient and does not model static-versus-dynamic friction transition, anisotropy, rolling friction, torsional friction or compliant materials.

Why a manifold needs persistent identity and sequential sweeps

A wide box can contact a floor at two corners. Both rows modify the same centre-of-mass velocity and angular velocity. Solving one row therefore changes the velocity seen by the next row. A one-pass independent pair of impulses is not equivalent to solving their coupled system. The reference witness stores two world-space contact points, evaluates each row in sequence, and repeats sweeps. The residual normal speeds and angular velocity are checked after twenty sweeps. Its iteration result is deterministic for its fixed row order but should not be advertised as an order-independent exact solution.

On the next frame, a geometry matcher must identify whether each physical contact feature persisted. If the same feature, body pair, contact orientation, and compatible basis survive, previously accumulated impulses are useful initial guesses. Warm-start once by applying the cached impulses to the newly constructed pre-solve velocities before iteration. Never warm-start twice, and never reuse a tangential scalar after rotating the tangent basis without transforming it. A changed feature ID, reversed A/B order, altered normal, teleport, or discontinuous mass/inertia change may invalidate the cache. The witness includes a feature ID as data but does not implement feature matching; that is a separate production requirement.

Caches may also require dt-aware scaling when timestep changes, and a true contact solver must decide how speculative contacts and missed or sleeping frames are handled. Warm-starting can improve convergence, but it is not a substitute for manifold quality.

Contact identity: why matching by memory address or contact index is insufficient

The physical reaction at a point can be reused between frames only if the cache still refers to the same interacting surface features. When two faces touch, clipping may produce two manifold points whose array order changes as the bodies rotate. If we cache impulse #0 against array position #0, a later reordering can accidentally apply the left-corner impulse at the right corner, creating a torque that was never physically demanded. A robust narrow phase should assign each contact a stable feature pair, for example an incident vertex/edge identifier and reference face identifier, with deterministic canonicalization of body ordering. These identifiers are geometric facts maintained by collision generation, not sequential indices assigned by a container.

The executable contact-cache witness concentrates on the subsequent policy rather than inventing a complete polygon clipper. The Key holds canonical body IDs plus two feature identifiers. The map stores the previously accepted normal and tangent impulse, its local normal direction, the previous friction coefficient, timestep, and last-seen frame. The cache is valid only if the same key was seen on the immediately preceding frame, the normal has changed by no more than 15 degrees, and the new timestep is between half and twice the cached timestep. These are documented laboratory thresholds, not universally optimal thresholds or engine-wide facts. The code rejects reversed body order because reversing A and B changes the sign of the normal and impulse convention.

A tangent impulse is a vector in world space, although this 2D solver stores it as one scalar relative to a perpendicular tangent. When the normal rotates from n_old to n_new, the tangent axes t_old=(-n_old.y,n_old.x) and t_new=(-n_new.y,n_new.x) also rotate. The old physical friction impulse is P_t_old=λ_t_old t_old. The scalar along the new tangent is its dot projection:

$ {t,new}^{seed} = ({t,old},t_{old}t_{new}). $

The normal cache receives the same heuristic timestep ratio, and the tangent is clamped to ± μ_new λ_n_new. With an old upward normal (0,1), the old tangent is (-1,0). If the normal turns 10 degrees, the tangent projection of a previous scalar impulse 0.5 is 0.5 cos(10°) ≈ 0.492404, while the world impulse direction has changed consistently. Reusing 0.5 unchanged would preserve the scalar but not the intended projection onto the new contact tangent. This linear projection is a warm-start heuristic, not an exact solution of the new contact constraint; the subsequent iterative solver must still correct its residual.

An edit to the friction coefficient clears only the tangential cached impulse in this experiment, retaining the normal impulse if all other validity rules pass. A material change in restitution, velocity discontinuity, teleport, substantial mass/inertia change, sleeping transition, or topology discontinuity may also require cache rejection in a production system and is not automatically detected by this small input type. Impulse scaling by timestep ratio is similarly a common starting heuristic, not an unconditional physical identity; the test exercises ratios 0.5, 1, and 4 and rejects the last. A caller must invoke begin_frame, use lookup to seed each new manifold row, warm-start those rows once, run velocity iterations, store each final impulse exactly once, and prune stale entries. Pruning at the wrong moment can erase still-needed contacts; storing duplicate feature keys silently makes iteration results depend on array ordering, so the witness rejects duplicates.

The implementation has a testable boundary: it assumes a reliable feature matcher has already produced identifiers, that contact validity has been established by the geometry system, and that stable body IDs are never prematurely recycled. A generation-counted body handle would be safer than an integer object index alone. The cache does not detect 3D tangent-frame rotation, it does not calculate a physically accurate contact point, and its ordered map is a reference implementation rather than a measured real-time allocation strategy. A production engine should benchmark a preallocated flat hash map or per-pair cache with explicit frame ownership and deterministic iteration requirements.

Velocity correction is not penetration correction

The equations above change velocities. They do not, by themselves, repair existing overlaps in positions. A production pipeline generally needs a distinct and carefully scoped policy: geometry generation and signed separation, speculative contact margins, split impulses or position-level stabilization, and consistent timestep handling. Naively adding a large position-error velocity bias can inject energy, make stacks jitter, or break restitution. This CPU witness intentionally has no position integrator, no Baumgarte term, no split impulse and no continuous collision detection. Therefore its passing tests cannot establish the correctness of CCD tunneling prevention or deep-overlap recovery.

From end-of-frame overlap to continuous time of impact

The contact solver described above only acts on contacts it has been given. A fast-moving disk can start to the left of a thin obstacle and finish to the right of it without overlapping at the end of a fixed simulation step. If collision detection samples positions only at the step boundary, it sees no collision, so even a mathematically perfect impulse solver cannot prevent tunneling. This is the reason continuous collision detection (CCD) is a separate geometric question: what is the first time, within the proposed integration interval, when the moving shapes touch?

For two disks with initial centres x_A and x_B, constant velocities v_A and v_B, and radii r_A, r_B, define the relative centre separation p = x_B - x_A, relative velocity v = v_B - v_A, and sum of radii R = r_A + r_B. Their separation at time t is p(t) = p + tv. They first touch when the squared centre distance equals the squared radius sum:

$ p+tv2=R2. $

Expanding the dot product gives the quadratic

$ at^2+bt+c=0, a=vv, b=2pv, c=pp-R^2. $

The meaning of the coefficients is crucial. c is the initial squared-distance gap: c<0 means the disks are already overlapping and this witness returns t=0, assigning overlap correction to a separate solver; c=0 means initial touching. If a=0, the relative geometry never moves during the interval. For initially separated disks, b≥0 means squared distance is not initially decreasing, so a collision cannot occur under these constant velocities. A discriminant D=b²−4ac<0 means the motion line misses the expanded-radius disk. D=0 gives a tangent or grazing touch, which counts as a contact in this laboratory.

The familiar quadratic expression (-b−sqrt(D))/(2a) can lose precision when nearly equal quantities are subtracted. The swept-disk CPU witness instead computes a stable intermediate q = -0.5(b − sqrt(D)) in its restricted b<0 branch, then evaluates the roots as t_near = c/q and t_far = q/a. Their product remains c/a, and the smaller root is tested against 0≤t≤Δt. The code uses std::fma in the discriminant to avoid one rounding step, but this is still finite-precision arithmetic; reliable collision detection across extreme dynamic ranges needs scale-aware error analysis or a more robust predicate policy.

Consider a disk of radius 1 m stationary at the origin and another radius-1 disk initially at x=10 m moving left at 100 m/s. Its centre must move 8 m before touching, so the time of impact is 0.08 s. At Δt=0.1 s, the moving disk would end at the origin and overlap if sampled; for an even faster moving disk it could end past the obstacle and be missed entirely. An analytical time-of-impact query reports the 0.08 s encounter regardless of the end position. During a simulation step, a practical engine can advance up to this impact, generate a contact normal, solve or schedule the event, and then advance the remaining time, with a bounded substep count and an explicit policy for simultaneous events and resting contacts.

The event’s collision normal is the normalized relative separation n(t) = (p+tv)/|p+tv|, pointing A to B. When initial centres coincide, there is no unique geometric normal; the witness uses a deterministic velocity-based fallback or +x if relative velocity is zero. This fallback is a test policy rather than a geometrically determined surface normal. The tests explicitly examine grazing touch, no-hit trajectories, hits outside the requested frame, existing overlap, coincident centres, invalid parameters, a high-dynamic-range trajectory, and Galilean invariance under equal velocity added to both bodies. The latter should not change relative motion or time of impact.

What this does not solve: disk CCD assumes translational linear motion throughout the interval and fixed radii. It does not include forces or acceleration changing the trajectory, rotation of polygons, concave meshes, vertex-edge events, general convex support functions, conservative advancement, broadphase swept bounds, contact island rescheduling, stable substep integration, or CCD after multiple impulses. It also does not prove the absence of false misses at all floating-point scales. These exclusions must be explicit when moving from a CPU analytic oracle to the engine’s full collision pipeline.

A complete impact event: geometry, first time, impulse and remaining interval

The earlier swept-disk query identifies an impact but does not evolve a scene. The independent disk event pipeline laboratory connects geometry, state integration, simultaneous constraints and the remainder of the frame. It does not claim to be Kairo’s actual world step. The model assumes fixed-radius, non-spinning disks, piecewise constant velocities, instantaneous frictionless impulses, and linear motion between impacts. There are no forces, torque, resting-contact stabilization, soft contacts or arbitrary polygons.

The entire algorithm follows from keeping one variable: remaining time. At each iteration, query all unordered disk pairs for their first collision in that remaining interval. If no pair collides, advance every position by its current velocity times the entire remaining interval. If collisions exist, find the earliest time, move all disks to that instant, collect other impacts at approximately the same time, freeze each event’s incoming normal velocity and restitution target, solve their normal impulses, then repeat the time-of-impact scan because the impulses have changed the future motion.

The numerical trace is visible in the first laboratory test. A radius-1 stationary disk is at x=0. Another radius-1 disk starts at x=10 with velocity −100 m/s, and the requested frame duration is 0.10 s. The moving disk must travel 8 m before the two surfaces meet, giving TOI=0.08 s. The world advances both disks through 0.08 s, then an elastic impulse against the infinite-mass disk reverses its incoming velocity to +100 m/s. The remaining time is 0.02 s, so its centre ends at x=4 m. An end-of-frame overlap test cannot reconstruct this physically meaningful trajectory by merely reversing the velocity at t=0.10 s.

For non-spinning disk collisions along the line of centres, the inverse effective mass is the sum of inverse masses, k = m_A⁻¹ + m_B⁻¹. With unit collision normal n pointing from A to B, relative normal speed u_n=(v_B−v_A)·n, and fixed impact target b=−e u_n_before, the solver’s unilateral accumulated impulse is

$ {next}=(0,{previous} + {m_A{-1}+m_B{-1}}). $

Only the difference Δλ = λ_next − λ_previous changes velocities. In a simultaneous batch, multiple contact rows may share a disk, so each row modifies the velocities seen by subsequent rows. The laboratory runs 32 sequential sweeps, freezing the original bounce target rather than repeatedly inventing a new restitution event. A symmetric three-disk scene tests two simultaneous impacts; another three-disk scene tests two impacts at different times in one frame.

The discovery procedure is O(n²) for each rescan because it checks every unordered pair, with no spatial acceleration. The same-time grouping threshold and near-touch geometry threshold are explicit finite-precision policies, not robust computational-geometry predicates. Grazing trajectories with zero closing normal speed are skipped. Deep initial overlaps are rejected rather than repaired. An event budget throws when exhausted, preventing an infinite event loop from masquerading as successful advancement. Importantly, a thrown exception can leave the input scene partly advanced: a production caller needs a rollback snapshot or transactional step if partial state mutation is unacceptable.

The nine deterministic tests exercise fast impacts, isolated elastic momentum and energy conservation, simultaneous row coupling, separating pairs, initial overlap rejection, event-budget exhaustion, chained events, ideal inelastic energy loss, and zero-duration/duplicate-ID validation. These tests establish a small analytic oracle, not a general proof of energy or convergence for arbitrary many-body simultaneous collisions, a guarantee against floating-point tunneling, support for rotating convex objects, or a persistent resting-contact engine. For an impact against an externally fixed body, momentum conservation of the two displayed disks alone is not the correct closed-system invariant; the stationary environment receives the reaction.

Reducing collision search without losing collisions: conservative swept bounds

The event-step laboratory above asks every pair of disks whether they will collide during the remaining time interval. With n bodies, this examines n(n−1)/2 unordered pairs after each event. For 1,000 disks, that is 499,500 expensive exact pair-time queries per scan—even if almost every disk is far away from the others. A broad phase exists to reject pairs that cannot possibly interact using a cheaper geometric test; it is not allowed to reject a true collision merely to be fast. This is why the central proof obligation is conservative coverage, not an attractive benchmark on one scene.

For a disk of radius r, initial centre p=(p_x,p_y), velocity v=(v_x,v_y) and remaining interval Δt, its centre under constant velocity travels along the segment from p to p+vΔt. Every possible disk position lies inside its swept axis-aligned rectangle. Its x bounds are min(p_x,p_x+v_xΔt)−r and max(p_x,p_x+v_xΔt)+r; y is analogous. The swept-broadphase reference lab conservatively rounds each boundary one representable floating-point value outward with std::nextafter. The exact continuous disk shape is a capsule around the segment, while its swept AABB is a larger rectangle: the rectangle admits extra pairs but must not discard any collision, provided the endpoints and bounds are correctly represented.

The algorithm sorts these rectangles by their minimum x coordinate, breaking ties by stable disk ID. As it visits each new rectangle, it removes from an active set any earlier rectangle whose maximum x lies strictly before the current minimum x. Every remaining active rectangle overlaps along x; the algorithm then compares their y intervals. Pairs that pass both checks are returned in deterministic lexicographically sorted index order, with a duplicate assertion. A true disk impact at time t∈[0,Δt] means the two disk regions intersect at that time; their swept AABBs must both contain the intersection point. Therefore their AABBs overlap in x and y and the pair must survive the broad-phase filtering. The reverse implication is false: AABBs may overlap even when the disks pass at different times or miss geometrically. The exact TOI narrow phase must therefore test every candidate before scheduling an event.

The laboratory compares its candidate set with an independent analytic disk TOI predicate, rather than comparing the broad phase against itself. Each true TOI pair must appear in the returned set. It tests a high-speed crossing, 100 stationary well-spaced disks with zero candidates, 200 seeded randomized scenes containing 35 disks each, and malformed identity/time inputs. The random scenes therefore examine up to 119,000 unordered pairs for conservative coverage, because each 35-disk scene contains 595 pairs. These are useful regression witnesses, not a proof against all finite-precision failures.

Sorting has O(n log n) comparison cost. Maintaining the simple active vector has potentially O(n²) scanning and removal cost when many broad AABBs overlap; the output itself can contain O(n²) candidate pairs in a dense scene. A scalable production version may use a better interval structure, broadphase BVH, grid, or incremental pair cache, and should benchmark temporally coherent motion rather than assuming this sample has production throughput. The original broadphase witness remains independently testable; the event stepper now has an optional swept-candidate mode alongside its exhaustive reference mode. Both generate candidate pairs for the current remaining interval, and the event stepper rebuilds candidates after each velocity-changing impact. A differential test source is committed to compare complete outcomes, but its successful GitHub-hosted execution remains unverified. This code-level integration is not yet native Kairo runtime integration or evidence of speedup.

How to reconstruct and verify the witness

Read the Row fields as a prepared contact Jacobian in compressed form: ra/rb are the lever arms, n/t are the constraint axes, kn/kt are scalar rows of the matrix J M⁻¹ Jᵀ. The method relative_velocity computes Jv, inverse_effective_mass computes a row’s inverse effective mass, solve_one projects impulse increments, and warm_start applies an already-owned cache once. make_row validates data and freezes the impact target. The six tests cover central momentum/energy, friction orientation, angular impulse, separating and static degeneracies, coupled two-contact iteration/next-frame cache, and nonfinite-input rejection.

Run strict compilation and execution, then run a sanitizer build. Expected output is persistent-contact witness: 6 suites PASS. This verifies only the tested cases on the compiling environment; the repository GitHub Actions workflow repeats strict and undefined-behavior checks, with remote status to be verified separately.

A reconstruction exercise is to add two bodies with unequal masses and an off-centre contact, compute kn by hand and compare every intermediate u_n, Δλ_n, Δv and Δω. A stronger follow-up exercise is to implement real feature matching, deliberately reverse normals between frames, and demonstrate that incorrectly reused cached tangential impulses generate artificial energy. Neither extension is presently claimed as implemented.

Verified boundary and research questions

The lab does not verify Kairo’s current renderer or physics engine, broadphase pair generation, narrowphase contact topology, 3D Jacobians, static/dynamic island management, precise multi-contact complementarity, numerical convergence across arbitrary scenes, determinism across compilers, robust CCD, or real-time performance. Before a research claim about stability or speed, define independent scene families, error metrics (maximum penetration, residual closing speed, drift, energy increase), iteration budgets, timestep families and order-randomization trials. Compare warm versus cold starts without changing geometry, feature matching or tolerances at the same time.

The three books contained approximately 23 links into the old archival volumes at the inspected head: 1 from Mathematics, 11 from Graphics and 11 from Game Engine. The source targets still exist, so these are mostly legacy detours, not missing files. Nevertheless they violate the spirit of one reader-facing continuous destination per subject. Those are often C++/shader syntax, escaped expressions, or images, not Obsidian page links. The Engine source insertion is particularly large and now occupies roughly forty thousand lines before the original mid-engine renderer material. Graphics also contains an early full XR source block. These are high-priority reading-flow issues even though the mechanical content-preservation checks are green. Preserve original words, but use linking, carefully justified section placement and substantive bridge explanations to make the story follow a recurring engine problem rather than a pasted source queue.

Implementation-depth contract for every developed concept

A reader should be able to close the book and build the mechanism. Therefore a concept is not “done” until its first meaningful use provides: the forcing engineering problem; definitions of every symbol, convention and unit; the derivation and its assumptions; the concrete memory/state representation and ownership; the full algorithm and decision branches; a complete documented implementation or a clearly labeled API-specific implementation; a numerical trace with inspectable intermediate state; failure/degeneracy and alternatives; proof of invariants and bounded behavior; and reproducible positive, negative and metamorphic tests. The note itself must contain these, not just a heading, a pointer to a video, or a code file that the reader must discover elsewhere.

Witness categories must remain distinct. A CPU-only pedagogical model can prove logic, arithmetic and expected rejection cases. It cannot prove production GPU memory visibility or Apple/NVIDIA driver behavior. A reference engine test cannot establish the current Kairo integration unless the exact Kairo commit and reproducible build are inspected. A mathematically derived assumption is not an observed result; a video transcript’s claim is not verified code; the 3,000-part route map is an ownership assignment rather than 3,000 completed reconstructions.

Current development increment: logical render-graph compiler

The Game Engine volume now carries a full C++20 pass-graph compiler inline at the point where renderer intent becomes backend work. The independent laboratory is tools/labs/render_graph_contract_lab.cpp, source-synchronized through tools/check_continuous_code_sync.py. It builds a DAG from per-resource last-writer and reader-cohort state, records RAW/WAR/WAW hazards, handles imported history, topologically sorts with deterministic tie-breaking, and rejects duplicate resources, uninitialized transient reads, feedback and explicit cycles. The six-pass G-buffer/shadow/lighting/temporal/tone-map/present trace and negative cases make those semantics inspectable. GCC and Clang compiled/reran the reference locally with -O1 and -O2 -DNDEBUG, warnings-as-errors.

Boundary: This is a single-queue logical whole-resource compiler, not an implemented Vulkan or Metal render graph. It does not emit stage/access masks, image layout transitions, queue-family ownership, timeline waits, transient aliasing or device-loss recovery. Those remain first-class milestones, not implicit features of this passing laboratory. See the Vulkan synchronization specification for the separate memory-model obligations.

Unit directions and safe normalization

Unit directions and safe normalization

Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: Phase6

Definition and mechanism

A unit direction is finite, nonzero input scaled to approximate length one. Scale by the largest absolute component before measuring to avoid unnecessary squared overflow or underflow. Zero has no direction; application noise thresholds are distinct from numerical existence.

For finite nonzero input, scaled squared length lies between 11 and 33. A vector of huge components can have a computable unit direction even when its original length does not fit.

Object construction and storage reuse

Object construction and storage reuse

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C007 · Latest development: C010

Definition and mechanism

Initialization creates an occupant whereas assignment replaces an existing occupant’s state. Ordinary constructor failure and post-target delegation failure have different complete-object cleanup behavior.

Storage needs sufficient size/alignment before object initialization can complete and start an ordinary lifetime. construct_at and destroy_at separate object life from backing storage. A cast alone does not construct arbitrary types. Some specified operations implicitly create implicit-lifetime objects; replacement and launder have additional preconditions.

M010 adds the resource-management view: placement construction or construct_at uses already-provided storage; it does not allocate that storage. destroy_at ends the occupant’s lifetime, while an arena separately decides when to reuse or release its bytes. Explicit destruction is safe only inside a protocol that prevents accidental second destruction. See Placement construction and explicit lifetime management.

Prerequisites

  • Storage duration and object lifetime — Backing-storage duration must be distinguished from the occupant’s start, destruction and replacement.

Used by

  • Object identity and generation handles — uses this prerequisite to establish its entity, lifetime, representation or lookup contract.
  • Return values and copy elision

ODE integration and stability

ODE integration and stability

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: Phase 9

Definition and mechanism

An ordinary differential equation gives the rate of change of a state over time. Forward Euler uses the current derivative: qk+1=qk+hf(qk,tk)q_{k+1}=q_k+h f(q_k,t_k), where hh is the time step. For decay u̇=−au\dot u=-au, it multiplies each step by 1−ah1-ah; if the magnitude exceeds one, the numerical solution grows even though the true solution decays. Spring systems can be stiff because high-frequency modes force very small stable steps. Backward Euler evaluates the rate at the unknown new state and is more stable for decay but requires solving an equation and may add numerical damping. Symplectic Euler updates velocity then position and often keeps energy bounded for conservative mechanics. Choose an integrator according to stability, accuracy, conservation, and runtime rather than displayed frame rate alone.

Phase 9–10 development

An initial-value problem consists of a differential equation and a specified starting state. A numerical integrator replaces continuous evolution with finite updates, so accuracy and stability depend on both method and step size. Consistency concerns local approximation, stability concerns error growth under repeated steps, and convergence concerns the limiting solution as the step is refined. Stiff systems can force explicit methods to take very small steps even when the visible trajectory changes slowly. Symplectic methods preserve Hamiltonian structure but do not generally preserve exact energy at each step.

Prerequisites

  • Absolute and relative error
  • Conditioning and singularity
  • ODE initial-value problems and stiffness
  • Time integrators and symplectic updates

Used by

  • Worlds, Images and Inference
  • Implicit differentiation and parameter sensitivities

Function contracts: domains, codomains, and images

Function contracts: domains, codomains, and images

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9

Definition and mechanism

A function is a rule that assigns exactly one output to every allowed input. Its domain states which inputs are valid; its codomain states the declared output set; its image is the subset actually reached. These sets affect whether an inverse exists and whether a formula is defined at a boundary. For example, squaring maps the real line into nonnegative outputs but is not one-to-one until its domain is restricted to nonnegative values. In a camera map, division by depth makes zero depth invalid, while a positive-forward convention further restricts visible points. Treating these as contracts makes composition safer: the output of one function must lie in the next function’s domain. A typed implementation can encode some, but not all, of these mathematical restrictions.

Prerequisites

  • No earlier concept node is required in this planned path.

Used by

  • Differentiation rules and chain rule
  • Partial derivatives and gradients

Derivative as a local linear map

Derivative as a local linear map

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9

Definition and mechanism

The derivative measures first-order change. In one variable it is the limit of the difference quotient; in several variables it is the linear map that best predicts small output changes near a point. For a scalar function, this local model is the tangent line. For a vector-valued function, it is a matrix acting on an input perturbation. The derivative is local: its approximation error becomes small relative to the perturbation as the step shrinks, but the linear model need not remain accurate over a large region. This view unifies instantaneous velocity, gradients, Jacobians, and optimization directions. It also gives a practical check: compare a small finite perturbation with the derivative’s predicted change, while remembering that floating-point rounding and curvature limit how small or large the perturbation should be.

Prerequisites

  • No earlier concept node is required in this planned path.

Directional and total derivatives

Directional and total derivatives

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9

Definition and mechanism

A directional derivative measures first-order change along a chosen direction. For a differentiable scalar field, it is the gradient paired with that direction; for a vector map, the Jacobian acts on the direction. The total derivative accounts for every input coordinate changing according to a path, combining partial derivatives with the rates of the coordinates themselves. A direction need not be normalized: normalization changes whether the derivative is per unit distance or per unit parameter. This distinction matters in signed-distance queries, motion paths, and parameterized camera projections. The total derivative clarifies the chain rule: if a state depends on time and an output depends on that state, the time rate is the local derivative composed with the state velocity. These are local statements, not global linearity claims.

Prerequisites

  • Partial derivatives and gradients
  • Derivative as a local linear map

Scalars fields and real-number models

Scalars fields and real-number models

Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: Phase6

Definition and mechanism

A scalar is an element of the field used by a vector space. A field supports addition, multiplication and nonzero division under specified algebraic laws. The reals also supply order and completeness. Floating-point values approximate this model but do not form a mathematical field.

An integer reciprocal need not be an integer; 2−1=1/22^{-1}=1/2. A real scalar can carry metres or seconds. A finite representation cannot preserve every real-number operation.

Vector spaces subspaces and span

Vector spaces subspaces and span

Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: Phase6

Definition and mechanism

A vector space is closed under addition and field-scalar multiplication with coherent algebraic laws. A subspace retains these operations inside a larger space. The span of generators is every finite linear combination of them.

The plane z=0z=0 is a subspace of ℝ3\mathbb R^3; z=1z=1 is an affine translate, not a subspace. The span of (4,0,0)(4,0,0) and (0,3,0)(0,3,0) contains all in-plane movements.

Barycentric coordinates and interpolation

Barycentric coordinates and interpolation

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

Barycentric weights reconstruct a triangle point as an affine combination. The weights sum to one; nonnegative weights describe points inside or on a nondegenerate triangle. Dot-system solves on off-plane inputs describe their projection, not proven surface membership.

The panel sensor (1,1,0)(1,1,0) has weights (5/12,1/4,1/3)(5/12,1/4,1/3) and corner temperatures (20,40,50)(20,40,50) interpolate to 3535.

University course development

Extend the existing interpolation note with the geometric meanings that make triangle rasterization and camera calibration easier to reason about. For triangle vertices p0,p1,p2p_0,p_1,p_2, a point inside can be written p=λ0p0+λ1p1+λ2p2p=\lambda_0p_0+\lambda_1p_1+\lambda_2p_2, where the weights sum to one and are nonnegative. Each weight is the area of the opposite subtriangle divided by the full triangle area; equivalently it is a signed edge-distance normalized by altitude. The weights therefore provide both a point-in-triangle test and attribute interpolation. They also reveal a limitation: screen-space weights do not linearly interpolate a 3D attribute after perspective projection. Interpolate reciprocal depth and attribute divided by depth, then divide the interpolated values to recover perspective-correct texture coordinates or colors.

Stereo correspondence and epipolar geometry

Stereo correspondence and epipolar geometry

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

Stereo reconstruction uses two or more views to infer depth from corresponding image features. A 3D point and the two camera centers define an epipolar plane; its intersection with each image plane is an epipolar line. Thus a feature in one image should match along a one-dimensional line in the other, reducing a 2D search to a constrained search. With calibrated cameras, triangulation intersects the two viewing rays; noise means they are skew, so estimate the 3D point minimizing reprojection or ray distance. Depth uncertainty grows rapidly when the viewing rays are nearly parallel, which happens for distant points or small baselines. Rectification rotates images so epipolar lines become horizontal scanlines. Occlusion, repetitive texture, and calibration error can still produce mismatches, so confidence and consistency checks are essential.

Prerequisites

  • Camera calibration and bundle adjustment
  • Barycentric coordinates and interpolation

Off-axis stereo projection and disparity

Off-axis stereo projection and disparity

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 11 · Latest development: Phase 11

Definition and mechanism

Stereo cameras use two eye centres separated by a baseline, while each projection frustum is shifted so a chosen zero-parallax plane aligns in the images. Parallel eye orientations with asymmetric frusta avoid the vertical mismatch and discomfort often introduced by toe-in cameras. For rectified pinhole cameras, disparity is approximately Δx=fxB/Z\Delta x=f_xB/Z, so inferred depth is Z=fxB/ΔxZ=f_xB/\Delta x under the calibration and rectification assumptions. Depth uncertainty grows roughly with Z2Z^2 for fixed pixel disparity error. Distinguish interpupillary distance from lens and display-centre spacing; the rendered baseline is an optical/comfort design decision. Use consistent pixel units for focal length, baseline, and disparity before computing metric depth.

Omnidirectional camera projections

Definition and mechanism

Cubemaps, equirectangular panoramas, and fisheye lenses map unit directions onto different image domains. A cubemap selects one of six faces and projects two direction components; equirectangular coordinates map longitude and latitude to a rectangle; fisheye mappings use a radial function of angular distance. These parameterizations are not equal-area: uniform pixel sampling does not imply uniform solid-angle sampling. Choose the mapping that matches capture or rendering needs, define face orientation and seam rules, and measure reconstruction with angular error between unit vectors. Fisheye formulas also differ (equidistant, equisolid, orthographic, stereographic), so name the model before interpreting pixels. At the poles, longitude is undefined, so seam and pole handling need explicit sampling rules.

Triangle rasterization and coverage tests

Triangle rasterization and coverage tests

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

Rasterization converts triangle geometry into a finite set of image samples. A pixel’s ideal coverage is the area fraction inside the triangle; a center test approximates this integral with one binary answer and therefore creates jagged edges. A directed edge defines an inside half-plane, so three signed edge tests classify a point against a triangle. A consistent tie rule assigns samples exactly on shared edges to one triangle, preventing cracks and double coverage. Supersampling tests several locations per pixel and averages their coverage, trading cost for a better area estimate. Hardware often checks candidate samples in parallel within a bounding box, then rejects or accepts coarse blocks that are wholly outside or inside. Triangle coverage is also the basis for interpolating depth, color, normals, and texture coordinates.

Prerequisites

  • Barycentric coordinates and interpolation
  • Sampling aliasing and reconstruction

Numerical error budgets

Numerical error budgets

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10

Definition and mechanism

A computed result can differ from a target because of model assumptions, discretization, solver termination, arithmetic, sampling, or uncertain reference data. These contributions may interact, so an additive budget is a diagnostic model rather than a universal identity. First identify which errors are deterministic bounds, which are observed estimates, and which are stochastic uncertainty. For example, a ray-traced pixel can combine approximation of geometry, finite sample variance, floating-point accumulation, and an imperfect reference image. Allocate effort where the dominant contribution lies: extra precision cannot fix model bias, and more samples cannot repair an incorrect PDF. Report units and assumptions with every tolerance.

Basis coordinates and dimension

Basis coordinates and dimension

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: Phase7

Definition and mechanism

Phase 7 stores basis images as matrix columns and derives coordinate conversion [v]C=C−1B[v]B[v]_C=C^{-1}B[v]_B. The endpoint bases and whether motion is active or passive determine the product; row-major storage does not. Reconstruction and active/passive example.

A basis is an ordered independent spanning set. Independence makes coordinates unique; spanning makes every vector reachable. Dimension counts basis elements over the chosen field, not stored components or bytes. A basis change alters coordinates without necessarily moving the physical vector.

(3,2)=1(1,0)+2(1,1)(3,2)=1(1,0)+2(1,1), so its slanted-basis coordinates are (1,2)(1,2). A plane inside three-dimensional coordinates still has dimension two.

Matrix norms and numerical error

Matrix norms and numerical error

The spectral norm is the largest 2-norm stretch and equals the largest singular value. The Frobenius norm measures aggregate squared entry energy. Residuals, orthogonality errors, and condition numbers need a declared norm and scale; a small residual alone need not imply a sensitive solution is accurate.

Use it when: setting scaled tolerances or interpreting numerical diagnostics.

Developed in Phase 8: The spectral norm measures worst-case amplification, while the Frobenius norm accumulates squared energy across entries. The chapter uses them to scale residuals, reconstruction errors, and orthogonality defects, and separates backward error in a nearby problem from forward error in the requested answer. norms and scale · residuals and error interpretation

A matrix norm can protect a geometry bound

A local sphere under a linear transform is generally an ellipsoid. The Frobenius norm times its original radius gives a safe, possibly loose enclosing radius. Taking only the longest matrix column can fail under shear. The culling example derives the bound, demonstrates the shear counterexample, and links its geometric figure. This connects numerical matrix norms to conservative rejection decisions.

Collision barriers and continuous detection

Collision barriers and continuous detection

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

A collision barrier turns a geometric safety condition into an optimization energy that rises sharply as bodies approach contact. Incremental Potential Contact (IPC) combines barrier terms for vertex-face and edge-edge separations with a time-step formulation that prevents interpenetration while a deformable object moves. Continuous collision detection (CCD) asks whether two moving primitives touch at any time during a step, not only at its endpoints; a pair can cross and separate between discrete samples. Robust CCD therefore needs conservative root bounds and careful handling of near-degenerate geometry. The barrier does not replace a correct collision set: missing pairs, invalid orientations, or a nonconservative CCD test can still allow tunneling. Very stiff barriers also make optimization ill-conditioned and require line search or step restrictions. IPC’s guarantees depend on assumptions about the initial configuration, collision constraints, and numerical tolerances. The core distinction is discrete overlap testing versus continuous-in-time contact prevention.

Extend the existing quaternion note with interpolation and sign handling in animation. A unit quaternion represents a 3D rotation, but qq and −q-q encode the same physical orientation. If two endpoint quaternions have a negative dot product, negate one endpoint before interpolation so the path follows the shorter arc on the unit four-dimensional sphere. Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: University courses

Plane reflection reverses a direction’s normal component. Refraction scales its tangent component by the incident/transmitted index ratio and solves for a unit normal component. Linear systems and fundamental subspaces

A linear system A𝒙=𝒃A\mathbf x=\mathbf b asks which inputs satisfy all row measurements at once. It is consistent exactly when 𝒃\mathbf b lies in the column space. The null space contains input changes invisible to every measurement; rank-nullity counts observable versus free directions.

Use it when: explaining consistency, underdetermination, least squares, parameter observability, or constraints in geometry.

Developed in Phase 8: The expanded treatment connects each row to a hyperplane and the complete matrix to a map: consistency asks whether the target lies in the column space, while the null space describes every invisible change to a solution. Exceptional projections and dimension

Exceptional projections and dimension

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

Projection usually lowers dimension, but a finite or fractal set may collapse unusually many points in special directions. For a finite planar set XX, count pairs whose orthogonal projections coincide in direction θ\theta; such pairs lie on lines parallel to the projection fibers. Averaging over directions gives a baseline, while exceptional directions produce larger fibers and encode geometric structure. For a density, the related transform integrates along each fiber, as in tomography; the Fourier-slice identity connects the transform of a projection to a slice of the original Fourier transform. Dimension and separation assumptions matter: finite point sets, thickened sets, measures, and finite-field analogues have different statements. A highly structured set can defeat naive random-grid intuition, and subfield examples in finite fields create strong obstructions. Results are estimates with hypotheses, not universal formulas for every dimension or projection family. This node connects geometric projection to incidence counting and harmonic analysis.

University course development

Computational geometry often decides whether points are left or right of a directed line, whether three points are collinear, or whether a point lies inside a circle. These decisions reduce to determinant signs. For points a,b,ca,b,c in 2D, the signed area determinant classifies orientation. If its exact value is near zero, floating-point rounding can change the sign and make neighboring algorithms disagree, creating flipped triangles or invalid topology. Robust predicates evaluate a fast approximate determinant with an error bound; if the sign is certain they stop, and if uncertain they recompute with higher precision. This adaptive strategy spends extra work only near degeneracy. It does not make constructed intersection coordinates exact, but it protects discrete branching decisions that must be globally consistent in triangulation, mesh repair, and ray-edge intersection.

Phase 11 camera development

Adaptive orientation and incircle predicates protect discrete sign decisions from floating-point error by refining arithmetic when an error bound cannot certify the result. Camera estimation has a different uncertainty: noisy pixels and weak observability can leave pose uncertain even when every sign is exact. Predicate robustness does not improve measurement accuracy, and a low reprojection residual does not guarantee every combinatorial decision was reliable. Keep layers distinct: use robust predicates for topology, uncertainty weights for image residuals, and Jacobian spectra for weak directions. Exterior products and geometric algebra

Exterior products and geometric algebra

Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: Phase6

Definition and mechanism

Exterior products represent oriented higher-dimensional elements without forcing them into vectors. A wedge is antisymmetric and bilinear; a bivector has grade two. Euclidean geometric algebra combines inner and exterior products into one product. Higher-dimensional sums of bivectors need not be a single plane.

The plane element I=𝒆1𝒆2I=\mathbf e_1\mathbf e_2 satisfies I2=−1I^2=-1, connecting plane rotations to complex-number behavior.

Local rigidity and mesh orientation fields

Local rigidity and mesh orientation fields

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

As-Rigid-As-Possible (ARAP) deformation seeks vertex positions that change as little as possible from a preferred local rigid transform. For each vertex neighborhood, fit a rotation to the deformed edge vectors, then minimize residuals between transformed rest edges and current edges. Alternating between local rotations and a global position solve makes a nonlinear shape-editing problem tractable, but the result depends on constraints, initialization, mesh quality, and rotation fitting. Instant Meshes uses direction or orientation fields over a surface to guide a quad-dominant remeshing; field singularities encode where a globally consistent direction cannot exist. A mesh’s half-edge connectivity, boundary structure, and orientation determine valid neighborhoods and field transport. Poor triangles, seams, boundary conditions, or inconsistent orientation can create artifacts. ARAP is a local preservation objective, not exact rigidity of the whole shape; a direction field guides topology but does not uniquely determine a good mesh without sizing and feature constraints.

Prerequisites

  • Half-edge mesh connectivity
  • Manifold polygon meshes and boundary structure
  • Subdivision surface masks

The panel is the convex hull of its corners. A filled disk is convex; its boundary alone is not.

Conditioning and singularity

Conditioning and singularity

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C004 · Latest development: Phase7

Definition and mechanism

Conditioning measures sensitivity to input perturbation. A=10−4I2A=10^{-4}I_2 has determinant 10−810^{-8} but condition number one in the 2-norm. Uniform scaling changes determinant magnitude without changing this conditioning measure.

Phase 7 develops κ(A)=∥A∥∥A−1∥\kappa(A)=\|A\|\|A^{-1}\|, near-parallel-column sensitivity, pivoted elimination and inverse residuals. Equal determinants can conceal very different stretch ratios: diag⁡(10−10,10−10)\operatorname{diag}(10^{-10},10^{-10}) and diag⁡(1,10−20)\operatorname{diag}(1,10^{-20}) both have determinant 10−2010^{-20} but conditions one and 102010^{20}. Full worked sensitivity example.

Subtraction of nearby inputs exposes input uncertainty relative to a small difference. Sensitivity belongs to the problem; exact subtraction of stored operands cannot recover information lost when those inputs were rounded.

Matrix factorization choices

Matrix factorization choices

Choose a solver from the matrix promises and task: pivoted LU for general square systems, Cholesky for SPD systems, QR for full-rank least squares, SVD or rank-revealing methods when weak directions matter, and iterative methods for suitable large sparse workloads. Reuse factors for repeated right-hand sides.

Use it when: choosing an algorithm before implementing or calling a numerical routine.

Developed in Phase 8: The factorization should follow the matrix structure and the requested result: LU handles general square systems, Cholesky exploits positive definiteness, QR fits full-rank least squares, and SVD handles uncertain rank and spectral questions. The comparison also weighs sparsity, reuse, memory, and whether an iterative tolerance is acceptable. factorization selection · the runnable LU example

PCA and covariance eigensystems

PCA and covariance eigensystems

Center sample rows, then find the orthogonal directions of greatest variance. For centered XX, SVD gives directions in VV, scores in UΣU\Sigma, and covariance eigenvalues σi2/(N−1)\sigma_i^2/(N-1). Units and feature scaling change the question; near-equal eigenvalues make individual axes unstable.

Use it when: describing point clouds, reducing dimensions, or estimating a best-fit plane.

Developed in Phase 8: PCA first centers observations so the covariance measures variation around the sample mean. The right singular vectors of centered data give principal directions, UΣU\Sigma gives scores, and squared singular values scaled by sample count give covariance eigenvalues; feature units and small eigengaps affect interpretation. centering and principal axes · plane fits and eigengaps

Phase 9–10 development: For a random vector XX with finite second moments, covariance is Σ=𝔼[(X−μ)(X−μ)T]\Sigma=\mathbb E[(X-\mu)(X-\mu)^T]. For every vector vv, vTΣv=𝔼[(vT(X−μ))2]≥0v^T\Sigma v=\mathbb E[(v^T(X-\mu))^2]\geq0, so covariance is positive semidefinite. Its eigenvectors give uncorrelated principal directions and the eigenvalues give variance along them. Whitening rescales nonzero-variance directions and needs a stated policy for zero or tiny eigenvalues. A Gaussian kernel used to model rendering footprints is a spatial distribution model, not automatically a statement about epistemic uncertainty.

Prerequisites

Eigenvalues and eigenspaces, Singular value decomposition, Symmetric positive-definite matrices and Cholesky. - Expectation, covariance, and dependence - Multivariate Gaussian distributions and whitening - Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse - QR factorization and least squares

Used by

Polar decomposition, Matrix factorization choices.

Eigenvalues and eigenspaces

Eigenvalues and eigenspaces

An eigenvector is a nonzero direction that a square linear map scales by its eigenvalue. The eigenspace is the null space of A−λIA-\lambda I. Real symmetric matrices have an orthonormal eigenbasis; general matrices may be defective or have sensitive eigenvectors.

Use it when: studying repeated powers, invariant directions, covariance, stability, or matrix functions.

Developed in Phase 8: Eigenanalysis begins with invariant directions, then distinguishes algebraic multiplicity from eigenspace dimension and shows why a defective matrix may not have a full eigenbasis. Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse

Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse

The exact SVD defines A+A^+ by reciprocating every positive singular value and transposing the orthogonal factors. A+bA^+b minimizes residual first and Euclidean solution norm among minimizers second. A numerical cutoff instead produces Aτ+A_\tau^+: if it discards a positive singular value, it solves a retained-rank approximation and can increase the residual of the original system. The cutoff makes the treatment of weak directions explicit.

Use it when: rectangular or rank-deficient least squares needs a minimum-norm answer.

Developed in Phase 8: The exact pseudoinverse reciprocates every positive singular value, yielding the least-squares solution with minimum Euclidean norm. A practical cutoff defines a different, truncated operator: discarding even a positive singular value can increase the residual for the original system, so the tolerance and retained rank are part of the mathematical answer. the exact pseudoinverse · truncation and regularization

Prerequisites

Singular value decomposition, Linear systems and fundamental subspaces, Matrix norms and numerical error.

Used by

PCA and covariance eigensystems, Matrix factorization choices.

Teaching path: pseudoinverse.

Polar decomposition

Polar decomposition

The right polar form A=QHA=QH separates an orthogonal factor from a positive-semidefinite stretch H=(A𝖳A)1/2H=(A^\mathsf T A)^{1/2}. The orthogonal factor may include reflection; singular matrices can make its completion nonunique. Symmetric stretch can include shear in the chosen coordinates.

Use it when: separating local rigid-like motion from symmetric deformation.

Developed in Phase 8: Polar decomposition factors a map into an orthogonal part and a positive-semidefinite stretch. The SVD constructs both left and right forms, separates reflection from a proper rotation, and gives the nearest orthogonal or special-orthogonal factor when the singular directions allow a unique choice; zero singular values leave completion freedom. left and right stretch · nearest proper rotation and ambiguity

Prerequisites

Singular value decomposition, Eigenvalues and eigenspaces, Determinants orientation and volume.

Used by

Constrained optimization and inverse kinematics

Constrained optimization and inverse kinematics

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: Phase 9

Definition and mechanism

Optimization chooses parameters to minimize an objective while satisfying constraints. Gradient descent steps opposite the gradient; Newton’s method also uses curvature, while quasi-Newton methods estimate curvature from gradient changes. Constraints may be enforced by parameterization, penalty terms, projection, or constrained solvers. In inverse kinematics, the parameters are joint angles and the objective measures distance between an end effector and its target. Forward kinematics maps angles to a hand or foot position; its Jacobian maps small joint changes to small endpoint changes. A damped least-squares step solves a stabilized linear system to reduce target error without exploding near singular poses. Joint limits, collisions, and multiple valid solutions make initialization and constraints important. The same framework applies to fitting cameras, deforming meshes, or matching image observations.

Phase 9–10 development

An optimization problem specifies an objective, variables, and equality or inequality constraints before an algorithm is selected. A gradient step uses first-order information; Newton and quasi-Newton steps add curvature, while line searches or trust regions control how far a local model is trusted. For nonlinear least squares, Gauss-Newton approximates curvature from the residual Jacobian and Levenberg-Marquardt damps the resulting system. Lagrange multipliers and KKT conditions describe constrained stationary points under their regularity assumptions. These local conditions do not by themselves prove global optimality.

Prerequisites

  • Singular value decomposition
  • Coordinate frames and change of basis

Exposure and sensor response

Exposure and sensor response

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

A camera sensor converts arriving photons into electrical measurements. Exposure depends on scene radiance, lens transmission, aperture, shutter duration, and sensor sensitivity; changing these settings trades motion blur, depth of field, noise, and saturation. A pixel integrates light over a finite area and exposure interval before quantization. Sensor wells have finite capacity, so highlights clip, while low photon counts have shot noise and readout adds electronic noise. ISO gain amplifies the signal and its noise rather than collecting additional photons. The recorded raw values are not yet display colors: white balance, color transforms, tone curves, and transfer encoding turn measurements into an image. A camera model must distinguish photon capture, sensor response, and display rendering to explain dynamic range and exposure choices.

Prerequisites

  • Lens optics and depth of field
  • Color encoding and linear-light operations

Storage layout, compute lanes and external buffer layout are separate contracts. SIMD may operate within one vector or across objects. AoS, SoA and AoSoA change access patterns. Alignment and padding must be measured; a spare lane is not implicitly valid homogeneous data.

One million twelve-byte vectors occupy four million fewer payload bytes than sixteen-byte vectors. A sixteen-byte load still needs sixteen accessible bytes even if one lane is discarded.

Pointer arithmetic and provenance

Pointer arithmetic and provenance

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C003 · Latest development: C008

Definition and mechanism

M008 adds null/object/one-past distinctions, same-array representable subtraction and round-trip limits. Provenance proposals are research, not adopted C++23 rules; byte inspection differs from arbitrary typed access.

A scalar member behaves as a one-element array for pointer arithmetic, not as an array containing adjacent sibling members. &x+1 can be a one-past pointer but cannot be dereferenced to access y. Actual array storage supports traversal; a span only views an already-valid range. Layout/size assertions do not authorize sibling traversal.

A pointer is a typed access path constrained by array bounds, alignment, and object lifetime, not merely an integer. Within an array, p+i advances i elements; one-past is permitted for traversal but not dereference. Byte views inspect representations; uintptr_t, when provided, is an integer conversion facility, not permission to access arbitrary storage.

Prerequisites

  • Addresses and virtual memory — Mappings give numeric locations their process-specific storage identity.
  • Storage duration and object lifetime — Access requires an object and backing storage that are still valid.

Destruction and partial construction

Destruction and partial construction

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C009 · Latest development: C010

Definition and mechanism

The destructor body precedes reverse member/base cleanup. Ordinary constructor failure destroys completed subobjects but not the incomplete whole; failure after a delegating target completed has a distinct cleanup case. RAII binds resource release to an owning object’s lifetime.

M010 extends the cleanup invariant to files, locks and native handles, and distinguishes destruction from external resource completion. A destructor can enqueue deferred release when an asynchronous user still holds the resource. Constructor failure remains safe when each acquired duty is immediately represented by a completed owner member.

  • Storage duration and object lifetime — Cleanup belongs to an occupant’s lifetime, not merely a numeric storage address.

Placement construction and explicit lifetime management

Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C010 · Latest development: C010

Definition and mechanism

Placement new or std::construct_at initializes an object in storage already provided by the caller; it does not allocate that backing storage. The storage must have adequate size and alignment. std::destroy_at ends an object’s lifetime but does not release the storage. A pool/container must track occupancy, partial construction, exactly-once destruction, and when reuse is permitted. Transparent replacement and std::launder have detailed preconditions; launder neither constructs nor revives an object.

Weak observation and ownership cycles

Weak observation and ownership cycles

Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C010 · Latest development: C010

Definition and mechanism

std::weak_ptr<T> observes a shared_ptr ownership group without increasing its strong count. lock() atomically attempts to create a temporary strong owner; the result is empty if the managed object is no longer alive. Replacing one edge of an otherwise all-strong ownership cycle with a weak observation can allow the strong count to reach zero. A check with expired() followed later by access is not equivalent to a successful lock().

enable_shared_from_this joins the already-established shared ownership group; it must not create a second shared_ptr control block from this.

constinit requires static initialization without making an object const. Dynamic initialization across translation units requires ordering care; explicit owners or function-local statics can provide a clear dependency path. Local-static first initialization is synchronized since C++11, but later calls/mutations still require normal concurrency rules. Initialization and shutdown dependencies are distinct.

Namespace-scope/static objects have program-duration storage. Initialized writable objects commonly use data-like regions; zero-initialized objects use BSS-like zero-fill, avoiding literal zeros in the executable. Some objects require runtime dynamic initialization; cross-unit order is a distinct problem from storage allocation.

Prerequisites

  • Storage duration and object lifetime — Access requires an object and backing storage that are still valid.

Used by

Update downstream uses when later chunks build on this concept.

Allocator fragmentation

Allocator fragmentation

Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C003 · Latest development: C003

Definition and mechanism

Internal fragmentation is unused space inside an allocated block, e.g. 37 bytes requested in a 48-byte class leaves 11. External fragmentation is free space split into holes incapable of satisfying one contiguous request, e.g. three separated 20-byte holes cannot supply one 60-byte block. Metadata overhead is an additional cost.

C003 teaching chapter · Part definitions · Dependency Map

Reconstruction depth

Fragmentation is wasted allocation capacity caused by request shapes and allocator policy. Internal fragmentation is unused space inside an allocated block because of alignment, size classes or rounding. External fragmentation is free memory split into pieces that cannot satisfy a larger request even when total free bytes are sufficient.

A game or graphics workload amplifies the issue because lifetimes are structured: per-frame temporaries, long-lived assets, streaming resources and transient staging data behave differently. Using one general heap for all of them can mix lifetimes and make reuse less predictable.

A useful experiment records requested bytes, committed bytes, peak live bytes, largest free span, allocation count and reuse over time. Frame arenas eliminate external fragmentation inside a frame by resetting wholesale; pools trade generality for fixed-size reuse; free lists require split and coalesce policy.

Fragmentation is not measured by “the process uses a lot of memory” alone. Residency, allocator metadata, page commitment and application-owned slack must be separated before choosing a remedy.

Page faults and demand paging

A memory fault requires OS intervention when current translation/protection state cannot satisfy access. Valid demand loading, zero-fill, or copy-on-write may install/alter mapping then retry. Invalid addresses or denied permissions may fail instead. A fault need not perform disk I/O; a TLB miss need not fault at all.

Serialization

Serialization

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C001 · Latest development: C006

Definition and mechanism

Serialization maps semantic fields to a specified byte sequence; decoding validates and reconstructs them. Width, order, version, bounds, and padding policy belong to that contract. A U8/U32-LE/U64-LE header occupies 13 bytes at offsets 0/1/5, independently of a native record’s possible 16-byte ABI layout. Packing removes some holes, not host dependencies. Publication and durability are subsequent operations.

M004 extension: a binary32 representation word such as 3F800000 can be serialized as little-endian bytes 00 00 80 3F. Raw-bit preservation retains signed-zero and NaN-payload differences; canonicalization deliberately merges them. Numeric equality does not imply byte identity. This is a format policy, not permission to change existing files.

M006 adds explicit schema/version/identity contracts, overflow-safe dimensions and resource limits, raw-word payload preservation, integrity coverage and a complete 52-byte demonstration. A native scalar writer is not automatically cross-endian stable.

Prerequisites

  • Interpretation contract — Representation, type, and lifetime must identify what object exists.
  • Fixed-width integer types — The representation width fixes byte count and valid shift range.
  • Endianness — Byte order tells how digit significance maps to sequence positions.

GPU workgroups and synchronization

GPU workgroups and synchronization

GPU execution has several scopes that must not be collapsed into the word “thread.” An invocation executes one logical shader instance. Invocations are grouped into workgroups for explicitly shared local memory and workgroup barriers. Hardware may execute smaller subgroup or SIMD groups inside a workgroup. Many workgroups make up a dispatch.

A workgroup barrier can coordinate invocations that participate in that workgroup. It cannot create a global barrier across arbitrary workgroups in the same dispatch. If an algorithm requires all blocks to finish phase A before any block begins phase B, use a mechanism that establishes that dependency: usually separate dispatches/commands with API synchronization, or a carefully designed device-wide primitive supported by the target model.

Execution barrier versus memory visibility

“Everyone reached the same point” and “everyone can now observe the required writes” are related but distinct contracts. APIs and shading languages expose memory scopes and semantics because a control barrier alone is not a universal cache flush.

The producer/consumer question is always:

  • what operation produced the bytes?
  • what later operation consumes them?
  • which execution scopes must be ordered?
  • which memory accesses must become visible?
  • which resource/subresource is covered?

Subgroups

Subgroup collectives can exchange values and perform ballots, reductions and scans without workgroup shared memory. They are fast but require care around subgroup width, inactive lanes and portability. An algorithm that silently assumes 32 lanes can break on hardware using a different subgroup size.

Shared memory and bank conflicts

Workgroup memory is physically optimized for cooperation but has finite capacity and bank structure. Tiling can reduce global bandwidth, yet an unfortunate address pattern can serialize accesses through bank conflicts. Register pressure and shared-memory allocation also constrain occupancy, so increasing tile size is not free.

Evidence boundary

The canonical notes now distinguish CPU semantic models from native hardware evidence. A CPU prefix-scan or render-graph test can prove dependency logic but cannot prove Vulkan visibility, Metal hazard behavior, subgroup width or driver performance. Hardware claims require validation layers, GPU capture/counters, and device-specific results.

Teach and reconstruct: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs#Let many invocations cooperate without inventing a global clock.

Related: Prefix scan and stream compaction, Shader buffer ABI.

Cache lines and memory bandwidth

Cache lines and memory bandwidth

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C001 · Latest development: C003

Definition and mechanism

Packing can place more logical values in each transferred cache line, trading arithmetic for lower footprint and traffic.

A cache line is the block moved between cache levels; memory bandwidth is bytes transferred per unit time. With an illustrative 64-byte line, byte-per-bit data stores 64 logical bits, while packed data stores 512. Real line sizes and performance must be measured for the target.

Prerequisites

Reordering 24→16-byte records reduces footprint, not necessarily measured traffic or speed. Field reordering and AoS versus SoA separates hot field arrays from full records; TLB caches translations rather than contents.

Half-edge mesh connectivity

Half-edge mesh connectivity

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

A half-edge data structure stores each undirected edge as two opposite directed records. Each record points to its twin, the next directed edge around its face, its origin vertex, its edge, and its face; vertices, edges, and faces keep one representative half-edge. Repeatedly following next visits a face boundary. Following twin then next walks around a vertex fan. This makes local neighborhoods and edits proportional to local degree rather than requiring a scan of every face. Correctness depends on invariants: twin of twin returns to the original, a half-edge is not its own twin, and next pointers form closed face cycles. The representation naturally assumes manifold connectivity; it can encode flips, splits, and collapses by changing a bounded set of pointers, but careless updates can break the cycles and corrupt subsequent traversal.

Prerequisites

  • Manifold polygon meshes and boundary structure

Quadric error mesh simplification

Quadric error mesh simplification

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

Quadric error simplification greedily collapses the edge with the least predicted geometric error. For each triangle plane with unit normal nn and offset dd, form v=(nx,ny,nz,d)Tv=(n_x,n_y,n_z,d)^T and K=vvTK=vv^T. A homogeneous point U=(x,y,z,1)TU=(x,y,z,1)^T has squared point-to-plane error UTKUU^TKU. Sum the matrices of incident planes at each vertex; an edge candidate combines endpoint matrices. Partitioning the combined quadratic gives Q(x)=xTAx+2bTx+cQ(x)=x^TAx+2b^Tx+c, whose stationary point solves Ax=−bAx=-b. If the system is singular or indefinite, test endpoints and midpoint and keep the least-cost candidate. After selecting a location, reject collapses that flip incident face normals. The metric is a local approximation, so topology preconditions and orientation checks remain necessary.
