Sampling aliasing and reconstruction

Sampling aliasing and reconstruction

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: XR01 · Latest development: Phase 10

Definition and mechanism

Uniform samples identify frequencies only modulo sample rate and corresponding real-signal equivalences. Strictly band-limited ideal reconstruction needs non-overlapping spectral replicas; exact-Nyquist phase is a boundary hazard. Prefilter before decimation.

Phase 9–10 development

Signal aliasing occurs when distinct signal frequencies produce the same sampled values; reconstruction then cannot recover which signal generated the samples without additional assumptions. Stratification, low-discrepancy sequences, and blue-noise point sets describe where samples are placed, not a guarantee that the signal is band-limited or that an estimator is unbiased. Each strategy still needs a valid support, probability weight, and reconstruction filter.

  • Fourier analysis and spectral phase — Frequency and phase reveal transfer, sampling ambiguity and structural loss.

Expanded teaching explanation · Independent coverage · Dependency Map

University course development

Sampling records measurements of a continuous signal on a discrete grid. Frequencies that differ by integer multiples of the sampling rate can produce the same samples, so the sampled values alone cannot identify which original signal was present. For ideal band-limited reconstruction, the signal must be restricted below half the sampling rate; equality at the limiting frequency needs additional phase and endpoint conditions. A real pixel also integrates light over area and exposure time, making its measurement a filtered sample. Prefiltering attenuates frequencies that would alias, while reconstruction estimates a continuous signal from the stored samples. Ideal sinc reconstruction has infinite support; practical filters trade computation, sharpness, ringing and residual aliasing. More samples reduce integration error only when their placement and weights match the intended pixel or path-space measure.

Probability density and change of measure

Probability density and change of measure

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: Phase 10

Definition and mechanism

A probability density describes probability per unit of a chosen measure, not probability at a point. A density pA(a)p_A(a) over area differs from a density pω(ω)p_\omega(\omega) over solid angle. When a mapping changes variables, its Jacobian converts density so total probability remains one: pB(b)=pA(a)|da/db|p_B(b)=p_A(a)|da/db| in one dimension, with the determinant of the inverse Jacobian in multiple dimensions. In rendering, choosing a point on a light and using its direction from a shading point requires an area-to-solid-angle conversion involving distance squared and the light’s projected cosine. Estimator formulas are only correct when the sampling density and integral use the same measure. This concept prevents missing factors in importance sampling, environment-map sampling, and camera-lens integration.

Phase 9–10 development

A density is meaningful relative to a measure and its support; its value at a point is not itself an event probability. For a continuous scalar variable, an interval probability is the integral of the density over that interval. Under a differentiable one-to-one change of variables, the transformed density includes the absolute determinant of the inverse Jacobian. Values outside the transformed support have zero probability. A mixed law can contain both point masses and a continuous part, so one PDF alone cannot describe every distribution. When a renderer changes a surface-area density into a solid-angle density, the geometric Jacobian must preserve the same probability.

Automatic differentiation and backpropagation

Automatic differentiation and backpropagation

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: Phase 9

Definition and mechanism

Automatic differentiation evaluates derivatives by applying the chain rule to the operations in a program. Each operation has a local derivative rule; composing the rules gives the derivative of the complete computation without symbolically expanding it or approximating it by finite differences. Forward mode propagates a tangent perturbation and computes a Jacobian-vector product (JVP), useful when there are few inputs. Reverse mode propagates sensitivities from outputs back to inputs and computes a vector-Jacobian product (VJP), making gradients of one scalar loss with respect to millions of parameters practical. Backpropagation is reverse-mode differentiation through a neural network’s computation graph. It does not remove numerical problems: nondifferentiable operations require conventions, saturated activations can yield tiny gradients, and an incorrect graph or reduction yields an incorrect gradient. Gradients are local sensitivity information, not proof of a global optimum. Finite differences remain a useful small-scale check, but cancellation and step-size tradeoffs make them a poor training method.

Phase 9–10 development

Forward mode propagates an input tangent through local derivatives and computes a Jacobian-vector product. Reverse mode propagates an output sensitivity backward and computes a vector-Jacobian product. These are chain-rule evaluations on the operation graph, distinct from finite differences, which perturb inputs and can suffer cancellation. The reverse pass requires a valid reverse-topological order and storage that remains alive until propagation finishes. Differentiating a converged solution uses an implicit equation and its local Jacobian; it is not automatically the same as differentiating every solver iteration.

Latent-variable models and generative flows

Latent-variable models and generative flows

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

Generative models describe how data could be produced, often by first sampling a latent variable zz and mapping it to an observation xx. A variational autoencoder (VAE) learns an encoder distribution q(z|x)q(z|x) and decoder p(x|z)p(x|z); its evidence lower bound balances reconstruction likelihood against a KL penalty that keeps the latent distribution tractable. A generative adversarial network (GAN) trains a generator against a discriminator, creating a game that can produce sharp samples but may be unstable or collapse to limited modes. Normalizing flows use invertible transformations so the data density can be computed with a change-of-variables Jacobian determinant. These methods solve different tradeoffs among likelihood, sample quality, latent structure, and optimization stability. Their assumptions matter: a VAE’s posterior family may be too simple, a GAN score is not a calibrated density, and a flow’s invertibility constrains architecture. Generated samples are not evidence that the model has learned the true causal process.

ODE initial-value problems and stiffness

ODE initial-value problems and stiffness

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9

Definition and mechanism

An ordinary differential equation specifies a state’s rate of change as a function of state and time. An initial-value problem adds the starting state; together they define the trajectory when existence and uniqueness conditions hold. Numerical integration advances approximate states through finite time steps. Stability concerns whether numerical errors remain controlled under repeated updates, not just whether one step is accurate. A stiff system contains modes with very different time scales; explicit methods may require impractically small steps to remain stable even when the visible solution changes slowly. Implicit methods can enlarge the stable step region but require solving equations. Consistency, stability, and convergence are distinct properties. A simulator should choose its step and integrator based on the dynamics, not merely the display frame interval or apparent smoothness of one trajectory.

Prerequisites

  • Definite integrals and the fundamental theorem
  • Eigenvalues and eigenspaces
  • Absolute and relative error

Used by

  • ODE integration and stability
  • Time integrators and symplectic updates

Bit casting and representation

Bit casting and representation

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C004 · Latest development: C006

Definition and mechanism

A same-size eligible bit_cast transfers representation, not numeric value. On the checked binary32 host, bit_cast(1.0f)=3F800000, whereas a numeric cast gives 1. Pointer punning is not an equivalent legal operation.

M006 separates representation copying, numeric conversion and endian coding. Eligibility does not validate arbitrary padding/target representations or establish a typed object in file-mapped bytes. Use initialized compatible scalars and explicit external encoding.

Rendering history validity

Rendering history validity

A temporal renderer reuses information from earlier frames only if that information still estimates the same target quantity at the reprojected location. “Previous frame exists” is therefore not enough. History needs a validity contract.

A history sample may become invalid because of:

  • camera cuts or projection changes;
  • resize or dynamic-resolution changes;
  • object transform discontinuities;
  • newly visible or disoccluded surfaces;
  • material or lighting changes;
  • estimator changes such as sample pattern, exposure domain or denoiser configuration;
  • resource reallocation or version replacement.

Reprojection is a hypothesis

Motion vectors or previous transforms propose a correspondence from current sample to previous sample. The renderer should test that hypothesis with available evidence such as depth, normal, object/material identity, velocity magnitude or neighborhood statistics.

A common failure is using a valid coordinate that points to the wrong surface. Bounds checking prevents memory errors, not temporal ghosting.

Versioned history

Treat history like a cache with a key. Relevant state changes advance a version or invalidate specific history resources. The render graph can then express that a temporal pass consumes history version N and produces version N+1.

This is also important for progressive path tracing. Accumulation belongs to a camera/scene/material/light/estimator state. If any target-defining state changes and old samples remain, the output converges to a mixture of different images.

Failure-oriented tests

Useful temporal tests include a hard camera cut, a moving foreground object revealing background, an emissive material changing abruptly, resize, FOV change, jitter-sequence restart, and an object whose ID remains but geometry changes. For each case, record which history samples should survive and why.

The existing render-graph witness proves logical resource dependencies, not temporal validity itself. Native renderer evidence should capture motion/depth/ID buffers and show the acceptance/rejection mask.

Teach and reconstruct: Continuous Notes/Game Engine - From First Frame to Living Worlds#Let a renderer evolve without losing resource ownership.

Related: Temporal reprojection and history validation, Reversed-Z depth contracts.

Render graph barrier lowering

Render graph barrier lowering

A logical render graph and an API synchronization plan are different layers.

The logical graph answers:

  • which pass reads or writes each resource;
  • which hazards create ordering edges;
  • whether the pass dependency graph is acyclic;
  • when a logical resource is first and last used.

API lowering answers:

  • what concrete stage/access state each use requires;
  • what image layout or resource state is required;
  • which subresources are affected;
  • which queue executes each pass;
  • what barrier, semaphore, fence/event, or encoder boundary realizes the dependency.

The repository already has tools/labs/render_graph_contract_lab.cpp for the first layer. That CPU witness proves RAW/WAR/WAW edge construction, deterministic topological order and several invalid-graph cases. It does not prove Vulkan or Metal memory visibility.

State machine per resource version

A practical compiler treats each write as producing a new logical version. A read consumes a particular version. For every concrete resource/subresource, track the last known backend state:

producer pass
queue
stage/access
layout or storage state
version.

When the next use requires an incompatible state, emit a transition whose source scope covers the prior access and whose destination scope covers the next access.

This versioned model prevents an important bug: a pass can read “history texture” while the graph accidentally associates it with the current-frame version rather than the previous-frame version.

Subresource granularity

Whole-resource tracking is simple but can over-synchronize. Independent mip levels, array layers or depth/stencil aspects may be used by different passes. Moving to subresource tracking requires interval/range splitting and merging so that state for mip 0 does not overwrite the state of mip 5.

The first correct implementation should prefer conservative whole-resource barriers over an incorrect fine-grained optimizer. Fine granularity is an optimization after invariants are tested.

Vulkan lowering

For Vulkan synchronization2, a transition record eventually becomes VkBufferMemoryBarrier2, VkImageMemoryBarrier2 or VkMemoryBarrier2 inside VkDependencyInfo, possibly combined with queue submission dependencies.

See Vulkan synchronization2 and resource transitions.

Metal lowering

Metal does not mirror Vulkan’s barrier vocabulary one-for-one. The backend should lower the same logical dependency into Metal’s encoder ordering, resource hazard mode, fences/events where required, and heap/lifetime rules rather than forcing Metal to imitate Vulkan object names.

See Metal heaps memoryless resources and hazards.

Verification ladder

A render-graph compiler should be verified in layers:

  1. dependency graph against a CPU oracle;
  2. resource-state transition plan against hand-written traces;
  3. Vulkan execution with validation enabled;
  4. Metal execution with GPU capture;
  5. cross-backend image/data parity;
  6. transient aliasing stress with deliberately overlapping and non-overlapping lifetimes;
  7. current production-engine integration.

The current branch now has stages 1 and a minimal Vulkan synchronization2 execution/Metal compile boundary. The deeper stages remain explicit rather than implied.

Implicit differentiation and parameter sensitivities

Implicit differentiation and parameter sensitivities

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9

Definition and mechanism

Implicit differentiation obtains how a solution changes when it is defined by an equation rather than an explicit formula. If a state satisfies F(y,θ)=0 and the Jacobian with respect to y is invertible, differentiating gives dy/dθ=−(∂F/∂y)⁻¹(∂F/∂θ). This can differentiate equilibrium states, constrained optima, and roots without unrolling every solver iteration. For a converged optimizer, differentiating stationarity and constraint conditions yields sensitivity equations, but active-set changes, nonunique solutions, singular Jacobians, and imperfect convergence complicate the result. Continuous sensitivity equations propagate derivatives alongside an ODE; adjoint methods can reduce cost when there are many parameters and few scalar outputs. These are modeling tools with assumptions, not a guarantee that every algorithmic branch is differentiable.

Prerequisites

  • Automatic differentiation and backpropagation
  • Constrained optimization and inverse kinematics
  • ODE integration and stability

Differentiation rules and chain rule

Differentiation rules and chain rule

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9

Definition and mechanism

Differentiation rules let us build derivatives from simpler functions. Linearity handles sums and constant factors; the product and quotient rules account for both factors changing; the chain rule handles nested mappings. For a composition, the derivative of the outer function is evaluated at the inner output and multiplied by the derivative of the inner function. In multiple dimensions, this becomes matrix multiplication of Jacobians in composition order. Elementary rules for powers, exponentials, logarithms, trigonometric functions, and inverse trigonometric functions follow from limits and implicit relations. These rules are the local sensitivity algebra used by automatic differentiation and gradient-based fitting. Each rule has a domain: quotient denominators must be nonzero, logarithms require positive arguments, and inverse trigonometric derivatives can become singular at boundary values.

Prerequisites

  • Function contracts: domains, codomains, and images
  • Limits and continuity

Definite integrals and the fundamental theorem

Definite integrals and the fundamental theorem

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9

Definition and mechanism

A definite integral accumulates a quantity over an interval, with sign and units determined by the integrand and integration variable. Riemann sums approximate this accumulation by weighted samples; under suitable regularity conditions their limit defines the integral. The fundamental theorem connects accumulation and differentiation: an antiderivative evaluates the net integral, and the derivative of an accumulated integral recovers its integrand when continuity conditions hold. This link explains why integrating velocity gives displacement and why a variable upper-limit integral solves a simple differential equation. Definite integral, indefinite antiderivative, and geometric area are related but not interchangeable ideas. The integration variable is a dummy variable, so name it distinctly from the endpoint. Integrals also form the target of Monte Carlo estimators, where measure and sampling density must match.

Prerequisites

  • Derivative as a local linear map

Used by

Finite differences and step-size balance

Finite differences and step-size balance

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9

Definition and mechanism

Finite differences estimate derivatives from sampled function values. Forward and backward differences use one-sided samples and have first-order truncation error; central differences use samples on both sides and usually have second-order truncation error for smooth functions. Making the step arbitrarily small is not always better: subtractive cancellation and evaluation noise grow as the step shrinks, while truncation error grows when it is too large. The useful step balances these effects and depends on scale, precision, and function noise. Finite differences are valuable for black-box sensitivities and gradient checks, but they are not automatic differentiation and can fail near discontinuities or branch changes. A numerical gradient check should compare directional derivatives, use scale-aware steps, and avoid interpreting one tolerance pass as proof that every derivative path is correct.

Prerequisites

  • Derivative as a local linear map
  • Absolute and relative error

Jacobians, pushforwards, and pullbacks

Jacobians, pushforwards, and pullbacks

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9

Definition and mechanism

The Jacobian is the matrix of first derivatives of a vector-valued function. It maps a small input displacement to a first-order output displacement, a forward sensitivity often called a pushforward or Jacobian-vector product. Gradients transform in the reverse direction by the transpose Jacobian, the pullback used in reverse-mode differentiation. These operations differ because vectors and covectors have different transformation rules. Jacobians compose by matrix multiplication and their determinants describe local volume changes. A Jacobian is local: it does not replace a nonlinear transformation globally. At singular points it can lose rank or become ill-conditioned, affecting inverse sensitivity, uncertainty propagation, and optimizer steps. State coordinate ordering and column-vector conventions before interpreting signs or multiplication order.

Prerequisites

  • Matrix multiplication and composition order

Taylor models and approximation error

Taylor models and approximation error

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9

Definition and mechanism

A Taylor model approximates a smooth function near a reference point using its value, derivatives, and higher-order terms. The first-order model is the derivative’s linear map; the second-order model adds curvature through the Hessian. A remainder term describes what the finite truncation omits, so local accuracy depends on step size and higher derivatives over the region. Big-O notation gives an asymptotic scale, while a concrete error bound needs assumptions such as bounded derivatives. Taylor models power local optimization, camera Jacobian updates, uncertainty propagation, and numerical error analysis. They are not reliable far from the expansion point merely because the polynomial is easy to evaluate. When the input distribution is broad or crosses a singularity, first-order covariance propagation can miss bias and tail behavior; validate or replace the local model.

Prerequisites

  • Derivative as a local linear map
  • Hessians and local curvature

Additive energy and approximate structure

Additive energy and approximate structure

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

Additive energy measures how often two pairs from a set have the same sum: E(A)=|{(a,b,c,d)∈A4:a+b=c+d}|E(A)=|\{(a,b,c,d)\in A^4:a+b=c+d\}|. A random-like set has relatively few repeated sums; a set with many additive coincidences often contains a structured subset. The Balog–Szemerédi–Gowers principle turns high energy into a large subset with small doubling, while Ruzsa-style inequalities and Freiman-type theorems describe how small doubling constrains approximate additive structure. In finite fields, sum-product results show that a set cannot remain simultaneously additively and multiplicatively concentrated unless it has special algebraic structure, such as subfield behavior. These implications are quantitative and depend on group or field hypotheses, subset size, and constants. High energy does not mean the entire set is a subgroup, and a small-doubling conclusion may apply only after discarding many elements. Energy is a counting diagnostic that guides structure theorems, not a complete classification by itself.

Interpolation versus approximation

Interpolation versus approximation

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10

Definition and mechanism

Interpolation reproduces every prescribed sample exactly, while approximation minimizes or controls an error criterion and may miss the observations. The distinction matters when data are noisy: a high-degree interpolant can fit measurement noise and oscillate between samples, while a lower-complexity approximation can better represent the underlying trend. In texture reconstruction, the samples themselves often define the represented signal, so interpolation is an appropriate reconstruction rule. In calibration, observations have uncertainty, so fitting a model may be more defensible. Neither method is automatically superior; choose based on the meaning of the data, the error measure, and whether evaluation stays within or extrapolates beyond the sampled domain.

Prerequisites

  • Taylor models and approximation error
  • Barycentric coordinates and interpolation

Used by

  • Tensor-product interpolation
  • Cubic Hermite interpolation
  • Bézier curves and De Casteljau evaluation

Named members versus array elements

Algorithmic stability

Algorithmic stability

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10

Definition and mechanism

A numerical problem can be sensitive even when an algorithm handles it well. Stability describes whether the finite-precision algorithm introduces only the error expected from rounding, often by showing that its output exactly solves a nearby problem. Backward stability is one useful form; forward stability asks directly how close the computed answer is to the exact answer for the original input. The claim must name its assumptions, arithmetic model, and problem class. For example, a stable linear solver can still have a large forward error on an ill-conditioned matrix. Stability therefore belongs beside conditioning, not in its place. A dot product with a small residual can still conceal an ill-conditioned problem, so report which notion of stability is actually supported.

Prerequisites

  • Forward and backward error
  • Conditioning and singularity

Used by

  • Bracketed and open root solvers
  • Numerical error budgets

Discretization, truncation, and roundoff

Discretization, truncation, and roundoff

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10

Definition and mechanism

Discretization replaces a continuous object or domain with a finite grid; truncation omits terms or limits an iterative expansion; roundoff comes from finite-precision arithmetic. They have different causes and respond to different changes. Refining a spatial grid may reduce discretization error while increasing computation. Adding more terms can reduce truncation error. Increasing precision or reformulating arithmetic can reduce roundoff, though a poor algorithm may still dominate. A signed-distance field sampled too coarsely can lose a thin feature entirely, while an ODE’s Euler step has a local truncation error even under exact arithmetic. An error budget should distinguish these mechanisms instead of calling every disagreement “numerical error.”

Bracketed and open root solvers

Bracketed and open root solvers

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10

Definition and mechanism

A root solver seeks f(x)=0f(x)=0. A bracketed method maintains an interval whose endpoints have opposite signs; continuity then guarantees at least one root remains inside, and bisection provides a predictable shrinking error bound. Open methods such as secant and Newton can converge faster near a well-behaved simple root, but they may diverge, encounter a zero derivative, or leave the relevant domain. A safeguarded hybrid uses a bracket for global protection and accepts fast proposals only when they preserve progress. Residual size alone does not certify root accuracy when the root is poorly conditioned, and discontinuous functions do not satisfy the sign-change guarantee.

Prerequisites

A posteriori error bounds for contractive iteration

A posteriori error bounds for contractive iteration

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10

Definition and mechanism

For a fixed-point iteration xn+1=G(xn)x_{n+1}=G(x_n), suppose GG is a contraction with Lipschitz constant q<1q<1 on a region containing the iterates and its fixed point. Then the remaining error is bounded by the next step divided by 1−q1-q: ∥x*−xn∥≤∥xn+1−xn∥/(1−q)\|x^*-x_n\|\le\|x_{n+1}-x_n\|/(1-q). The assumption is essential; a small step alone does not prove convergence because stagnation or a failed update can also make changes tiny. In implementation, report the contraction evidence or a suitable residual bound and keep failure distinct from success. This turns an observed update into a conditional, checkable estimate rather than a guess. If q=1/2q=1/2 and the latest step is 10−610^{-6}, this bound is 2×10−62\times10^{-6}, conditional on the contraction proof.

Convergence order and Richardson extrapolation

Convergence order and Richardson extrapolation

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10

Definition and mechanism

If an approximation has leading error Qh=Q*+Chp+O(hp+1)Q_h=Q^*+Ch^p+O(h^{p+1}), halving the step reduces that term by about 2p2^p. Comparing results at hh, h/2h/2, and h/4h/4 estimates the observed order; Richardson extrapolation combines two resolutions to cancel the leading term when the assumed order is valid. The method is diagnostic, not magic: measurements must be in the asymptotic regime, the same mathematical quantity must be computed at each resolution, and roundoff or stochastic noise must not dominate. For Euler integration, first-order refinement predicts the leading error to halve. Record the sequence and residuals rather than reporting an order from one pair alone. Ratios near an expected power provide evidence, but one noisy ratio is not a convergence study.

Reproducible numerical benchmarking

Reproducible numerical benchmarking

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10

Definition and mechanism

A useful numerical benchmark separates sample-level variability from run-level variability and pairs competing methods on the same inputs or seeds. Record the algorithm, precision, compiler/runtime settings, sample count, seed or keyed input, warm-up policy, timing method, and error metric. Compare distributions or paired differences rather than a single favorable run. A speed improvement is meaningful only if accuracy and failure rates remain acceptable for the target workload. For Monte Carlo methods, repeat independent runs and report uncertainty; for deterministic solvers, use analytical or manufactured solutions and measure convergence. Reproducibility is an experimental contract, not merely a fixed random seed. If the workload is stochastic, compare paired seeds and report both runtime and error distributions.

Spline bases and curve evaluation

Spline bases and curve evaluation

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

A spline is a piecewise polynomial curve whose neighboring pieces join under explicit continuity constraints. A cubic Bézier segment uses four control points and Bernstein weights; the weights sum to one, so the curve lies in their convex hull. A B-spline uses local basis functions so moving one control point changes only nearby spans rather than the whole curve. Knots mark where polynomial pieces meet; repeated knots reduce continuity. Catmull–Rom curves interpolate their control points and can be convenient for motion paths, while Bézier curves expose endpoint tangents through their handles. To evaluate a curve, compute basis weights at parameter tt and take their weighted sum of control points. Position, first derivative, and parameterization speed matter separately: even a smooth path may speed up or slow down unless its parameter is adjusted.

PDE fields and discrete Laplacians

PDE fields and discrete Laplacians

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

A partial differential equation constrains a field through spatial and temporal derivatives. Laplace’s equation Δu=0\Delta u=0 seeks a harmonic field whose value matches its neighborhood average; Poisson’s equation adds a source term. On a regular grid, finite differences produce the five-point stencil with four neighbor weights and a negative center weight. On a triangle mesh, cotangent weights encode angles and a mass matrix normalizes by vertex area. Boundary conditions supply essential data: Dirichlet fixes values, Neumann fixes normal flux, and Robin combines them. Neumann Laplace systems require zero net flux and a pinned value or mean because constants lie in the nullspace. Explicit heat updates have a stability-limited time step; implicit updates solve a sparse system. PDE algorithms separate field representation, spatial operator, boundary conditions, and time integration.

University course development

Extend the existing frequency-domain treatment with visual interpretation and filtering consequences. A Fourier coefficient records how strongly a sinusoidal basis function occurs at a given frequency and phase. In images, the origin of a two-dimensional spectrum represents slow spatial variation; moving farther from it corresponds to finer variation. A broad bright center indicates low-frequency structure, while energy far from the center often represents edges and texture. Filtering multiplies each frequency by the filter response: a low-pass response suppresses fine detail, and a high-pass response emphasizes it. Aliasing folds unresolved high frequencies into lower ones because sampled sinusoids can share identical sample values. This explains moiré patterns and animated shimmer, and shows why a spectrum is useful for diagnosing sampling problems rather than only for theoretical signal processing.

Hessians and local curvature

Hessians and local curvature

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9

Definition and mechanism

The Hessian collects second partial derivatives of a scalar objective. It describes how the gradient changes and supplies the quadratic term in a local Taylor model. For a smooth scalar field, the Hessian is symmetric under the usual equality-of-mixed-partials assumptions. Its eigenvectors indicate local curvature directions: positive eigenvalues give upward curvature, negative values downward curvature, and near-zero values weakly constrained directions. A positive-definite Hessian supports a strict local minimum in the unconstrained setting, while an indefinite Hessian signals a saddle-like local model. The Hessian is not the same as the curvature of an embedded geometric surface, though both involve second-order change. In optimization, exact Newton steps solve with the Hessian; practical methods may regularize or approximate it because conditioning, cost, or indefiniteness can make direct steps unreliable.

  • Symmetric positive-definite matrices and Cholesky

Multivariate Gaussian distributions and whitening

Multivariate Gaussian distributions and whitening

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10

Definition and mechanism

A multivariate Gaussian is determined by a mean vector and a symmetric positive-semidefinite covariance matrix. When the covariance is positive definite, its density is an elliptical bell whose principal directions are covariance eigenvectors. Cholesky factorization maps independent standard-normal samples into correlated samples; whitening applies an inverse factor to express observations in unit-variance coordinates. Singular covariance instead confines the distribution to a lower-dimensional affine subspace and has no ordinary density with respect to full-dimensional volume. Covariance transforms as AΣAᵀ under a linear map and approximately as JΣJᵀ through a nonlinear map near a reference point. These equations support sensor fusion and projected uncertainty, but a Gaussian rendering kernel is not automatically a normalized probability density or epistemic uncertainty model.

Nonlinear least squares: Gauss-Newton and Levenberg-Marquardt

Nonlinear least squares: Gauss-Newton and Levenberg-Marquardt

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9

Definition and mechanism

Nonlinear least squares minimizes one half the squared norm of a residual vector. Its gradient and Hessian involve the residual Jacobian; the exact Hessian also contains second derivatives of each residual. Gauss–Newton drops those latter terms, producing a positive-semidefinite normal matrix and an efficient local step when residuals are small or the model is close to linear. Levenberg–Marquardt adds damping to control ill-conditioned or overly aggressive steps, blending Gauss–Newton with gradient descent. These algorithms are useful for camera calibration, bundle adjustment, and geometric fitting. Residual scaling, parameter units, rank deficiency, and gauge freedoms influence the solution. Normal equations can square the condition number, so QR or other structured solves may be safer. A small residual does not prove parameters are identifiable or physically correct.

Prerequisites

  • Jacobians, pushforwards, and pullbacks
  • Hessians and local curvature
  • Symmetric positive-definite matrices and Cholesky
  • Constrained optimization and inverse kinematics

Stable quadratic root evaluation

Stable quadratic root evaluation

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10

Definition and mechanism

The direct quadratic formula can lose nearly all significant digits in one root when it subtracts nearly equal values. For real coefficients with nonzero leading coefficient and a valid nonnegative discriminant, compute a signed large-magnitude numerator first: q=−12(b+copysign⁡(b2−4ac,b))q=-\frac12(b+\operatorname{copysign}(\sqrt{b^2-4ac},b)), then obtain roots as q/aq/a and c/qc/q. The second root follows from the product relation x1x2=c/ax_1x_2=c/a. This avoids cancellation in the small root, but it does not prevent overflow in the discriminant or cover degenerate coefficients, nonfinite inputs, or q=0q=0; a robust solver also scales inputs and handles those cases explicitly. For example, the small root of x2+108x+1=0x^2+10^8x+1=0 is near −10−8-10^{-8}, exactly the root most endangered by direct subtraction.

LU factorization and reusable solves

LU factorization and reusable solves

LU stores elimination as triangular factors. With row pivoting in this vault’s convention, PA=LUPA=LU; apply the same permutation to each right-hand side, then solve one lower- and one upper-triangular system. Factorization cost is amortized across repeated solves.

Expectation, covariance, and dependence

Expectation, covariance, and dependence

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10

Definition and mechanism

Expectation is the probability-weighted average of a random quantity, and variance is the expected squared deviation from that average. Covariance measures how two centered quantities vary together; correlation scales it to a unitless linear-association measure. For a random vector, the covariance matrix is symmetric positive semidefinite because every directional quadratic form equals a variance. Zero covariance does not usually imply independence, except under special joint Gaussian conditions. Conditional expectation and total-variance identities decompose uncertainty into within-group spread and variation between group means. These moments drive Monte Carlo error analysis, Gaussian geometry, and linear uncertainty propagation. An empirical covariance depends on sample convention and denominator; Bessel correction concerns unbiased population-variance estimation under IID sampling, not a universal change to descriptive covariance.

Prerequisites

  • Probability spaces, events, and conditioning
  • Random variables and probability laws

  • Confidence intervals and sequential evidence
  • Monte Carlo rendering estimators and variance

  • PCA and covariance eigensystems

Perception feedback and robot learning

Perception feedback and robot learning

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

A robot learning system closes a loop: sensors produce observations, a policy chooses an action, the world changes, and new observations arrive. A policy maps states or observations to actions; a value function estimates expected future return and can help compare actions. Reinforcement learning updates behavior from outcomes, while imitation learning fits demonstrations. In visual robotics, the observation pipeline may include cameras, learned features, pose estimates, and spatial grounding; errors then affect movement rather than only a label. The training and deployment distributions can differ because the robot’s own actions change what it sees. Small perception errors can compound into different states and larger future errors, a form of covariate or distribution shift. Stable deployment therefore needs calibrated sensing, feedback timing, safety constraints, and evaluation on physical conditions. Demonstrations in simulation do not establish robust real-world manipulation; embodiment, contact, latency, and unmodeled dynamics matter. A successful policy is evidence for a task and setting, not general intelligence.

  • Contrastive vision and image-language alignment

Newton and quasi-Newton optimization

Newton and quasi-Newton optimization

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9

Definition and mechanism

Newton’s method builds a local quadratic model of an objective from its gradient and Hessian, then solves for the model’s stationary point. Near a well-conditioned solution with suitable smoothness and curvature, it can converge faster than gradient descent. Away from that regime, the Hessian may be indefinite, poorly scaled, or a poor model over the proposed step. Line searches and trust regions control step acceptance. Quasi-Newton methods such as BFGS estimate curvature from successive parameter and gradient changes, avoiding repeated exact Hessian construction. Their guarantees depend on assumptions and update safeguards. Optimization should monitor objective change, gradient norm, step size, constraints, and numerical failures; a small step alone can indicate stagnation rather than success. The method’s result is a local solution unless global structure proves more.

Prerequisites

  • Hessians and local curvature
  • Constrained optimization and inverse kinematics

University course development

Extend the existing color note with why image-processing arithmetic must distinguish encoded values from light. A display encoding such as sRGB uses a nonlinear transfer curve so code values allocate precision in a way that suits perception and storage. Averaging or adding those encoded numbers does not generally average or add emitted light. Decode to linear-light RGB before blending, filtering, estimating radiance, or compositing, then encode for display. If two equal-area samples contain linear intensities 00 and 11, their physical average is 0.50.5; averaging their encoded sRGB values and treating that result as light yields a different, brighter answer. Color primaries and a white point also define the coordinate system of RGB, so a numeric triplet is incomplete without its color space. Keep scene-referred radiance, display-referred color, and perceptual appearance separate.

Null pointers and optional access

Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C008 · Latest development: C008

Definition and mechanism

Prerequisites

Recall and next depth

Source and navigation

Teaching explanation and examples · Exact coverage · Dependency Map

Absence must be part of the type or contract

A null pointer represents “no object at this address-bearing interface”; dereferencing it is invalid. That makes raw pointer nullability an API question. If a parameter must always designate an object, a reference or explicitly non-null wrapper communicates more than a nullable pointer plus a comment.

Optional ownership and optional observation are different. A std::unique_ptr<T> may be empty while also owning when nonempty; T* may be nullable but usually says nothing about ownership; std::optional<T> stores an optional value without indirection. Choosing among them should follow lifetime and absence semantics rather than syntax convenience.

Null checks also do not prove lifetime. A non-null dangling pointer is still invalid, and a pointer can become logically stale even if its numeric address is later reused for a different object.

Tests for optional APIs should cover absent state, present state, transitions between them, moved-from ownership and invalid external identifiers. Avoid sentinel pointer values other than the language-defined null representation unless a low-level ABI explicitly owns that convention.

Ordering and bias

Offset-binary represents signed values by adding a fixed bias before storing an unsigned code:

q=x+B.q=x+B.

With an nn-bit field and the common midpoint bias B=2n−1B=2^{n-1}, the smallest signed value maps near code zero and the largest maps near the all-ones code. Unlike two’s complement, the unsigned lexical order of codes then matches the numeric order of represented values. That property is useful in some exponent fields, ADC outputs, sortable binary formats and hardware interfaces.

The bias is part of the format contract. Decoding with the wrong bias shifts every value while still producing plausible numbers. The IEEE-754 exponent field is related but reserves all-zero and all-one exponent codes for subnormals/zero and infinities/NaNs, so it is not simply an unrestricted offset-binary integer.

Tests should check both endpoints, the code corresponding to numeric zero, monotonic ordering, and rejection or handling of reserved codes when the surrounding format defines them.

Integrity and authenticity

Integrity and authenticity

Curriculum depth: Derived with executable primitive witnesses · First seen: C006 · Latest development: Phase 28 repair

Integrity means detecting unauthorized or accidental modification relative to a trusted reference. Authenticity additionally answers who or what was authorized to create the message.

Hashing a file and storing the digest beside it protects against accidental corruption only when the digest itself is trusted. An attacker able to replace both can recompute the hash.

A message authentication code solves a different problem: parties share a secret key KK and compute a tag such as

HMAC⁡K(m). \operatorname{HMAC}_K(m).

Someone without the key should not be able to forge a valid tag for a modified message under the security assumptions of HMAC and the underlying hash.

A digital signature separates signing and verification keys and supports different trust models. The choice between MAC and signature is therefore architectural, not a matter of which API call is available.

HMAC construction

For hash block size BB, normalize key KK to one block, then compute

HMAC⁡K(m)=H((K⊕opad)∥H((K⊕ipad)∥m)). \operatorname{HMAC}_K(m) = H((K\oplus opad)\,\|\, H((K\oplus ipad)\,\|\,m)).

The inner and outer domains prevent the construction from being equivalent to a naive hash of key concatenated with message.

tools/labs/crypto_primitives_lab.cpp checks HMAC-SHA256 against an RFC 4231 known-answer vector.

Key management is part of authenticity

A mathematically correct MAC does not help if:

  • the key is embedded publicly in the executable;
  • keys are reused across incompatible protocols without domain separation;
  • a compromised key is never rotated;
  • comparison leaks useful timing information in an adversarial environment;
  • replayed old authenticated messages are accepted without nonce/counter/version policy.

Cryptographic primitives are building blocks, not complete protocols.

Production boundary

The educational implementations in this repository exist to make the bytes/rounds/contracts reconstructable. Production systems should use vetted cryptographic libraries and platform key-storage facilities rather than treating a teaching SHA/HMAC implementation as hardened security code.

Related: Checksums CRCs and hashes, HMAC and HKDF, Merkle trees and authenticated structure, Shamir secret sharing.

Definition and mechanism

Narrow integral operands promote to int when it represents their entire range, otherwise to unsigned int; the operator acts at that promoted width.

Narrow integer types become int if int represents every original value; otherwise they become unsigned int. Promotion happens before the operation, not only on assignment. On the usual host, uint8_t{250}+uint8_t{10} is int 260; converting afterward to uint8_t yields 4.

IEEE-754 floating point

IEEE-754 floating point

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C001 · Latest development: C005

Definition and mechanism

IEEE-754 specifies floating formats and behavior including representation classes, rounding directions and exception conditions. A finite bit pattern is interpreted through sign, exponent and significand rules, not as a two’s-complement integer.

Binary32 has 1/8/23 stored fields and 24-bit normal precision; binary64 has 1/11/52 fields and 53-bit normal precision. Word 412A0000 encodes 10.625 in binary32. Exponent-zero and all-one fields distinguish zero/subnormal and infinity/NaN. Normal spacing expands with exponent; nearest-even and directed modes choose representable results under explicit rules. These format names do not prove every C++ float/double has those representations.

M005 develops alignment, cancellation, FMA and accumulated error. Numeric equality is not representation identity, and moving rounding points can change the computed result.

Prerequisites

  • Bit field — A field is a declared range with offset s and width w, not automatically a C++ language bit-field member.
  • Interpretation contract — For 0xAD, unsigned interpretation gives 173; eight-bit two’s complement gives −83.

A larger page covers more bytes per translation. With T same-size cached entries, illustrative reach is T×P bytes. One GiB requires 262144 pages at 4 KiB versus 512 at 2 MiB. Larger pages trade flexibility, availability, fragmentation and fault granularity; the counts alone do not prove performance improvement.

  • Allocator fragmentation — Coarser allocation granularity introduces space/availability trade-offs.

Source and navigation

C003 teaching chapter · Part definitions · Dependency Map

Reach, fragmentation, and measurement

TLB reach is approximately the number of cached translations multiplied by the page size. If a TLB can hold NN translations, switching from 4 KiB pages to 2 MiB huge pages can increase the bytes covered by those translations by a factor of 512.

That does not make huge pages universally faster. They can increase internal fragmentation, make allocation/compaction harder, change NUMA placement behavior and waste memory when only small portions of each huge page are touched. Transparent Huge Pages may also promote or split mappings asynchronously, so an application should not infer actual page size from its allocation API alone.

The right benchmark holds the useful computation fixed while varying working-set size and access stride, then observes TLB/page-walk counters where available. A speedup from huge pages should correlate with translation pressure rather than simply with a different allocator or cache footprint.

For engines, huge pages are most plausible for stable, large, densely accessed arenas—not as a default for every allocation.

Copy-on-write

Copy-on-write

Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C003 · Latest development: C003

Definition and mechanism

COW initially shares physical contents while deferring private copies. A permitted write to a COW-protected mapping faults; OS allocates/copies a frame, updates the writer’s mapping, and retries. Other mappings retain old contents. Not every read-only page is COW, so not every write fault is recoverable.

Prerequisites

  • Page faults and demand paging — Deferred private copying is implemented through a recoverable write fault.

Update downstream uses when later chunks build on this concept.

Recall and next depth

Pending: Fork behavior, mapping flags, reference tracking and costs.

Source and navigation

C003 teaching chapter · Part definitions · Dependency Map

Reconstruction depth

Copy-on-write delays physical copying until shared data is actually modified. At the virtual-memory level, two address spaces may initially map the same physical page as read-only. A write triggers a protection fault; the operating system allocates a private page, copies old contents, updates the writer’s page table and resumes the instruction.

The key invariant is logical independence after a write, even though physical storage was shared before it. This is why process creation can be cheap initially without eagerly duplicating every writable page.

COW has costs that disappear in a high-level description: the first write can incur a page fault and page copy, dirty-page accounting changes, and large working sets can turn an initially cheap clone into substantial later memory traffic. Huge pages and NUMA placement make those costs workload-dependent.

Do not generalize OS page COW into a recommendation for C++ value types. Library-level copy-on-write strings or containers complicate iterator/reference validity, threading and mutation semantics. The mechanism is useful when ownership and fault or copy behavior are explicit.

int need not be32 bits; sizeof(char)==1 measures a C++ byte and CHAR_BIT is at least8. Plain char is distinct from signed/unsigned char and its signedness is implementation-defined. size_t represents object sizes, not a stable serialized field. Query numeric_limits for digits, lowest, max and floating capabilities. A container’s size_type is not universally required to be exactly size_t.

<cstdint> exact-width types express binary layout contracts; least and fast families have different portability goals.

When supplied, std::uint32_t has exactly 32 bits; uint_least32_t has at least 32; uint_fast32_t is chosen for speed with at least 32. Exact-width typedefs are optional on implementations lacking suitable types. size_t represents object sizes and ptrdiff_t differences.

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C001 · Latest development: C003

Checksums CRCs and hashes

Checksums, CRCs, and hashes

Curriculum depth: Reference implemented and known-answer tested · First seen: C006 · Latest development: Phase 28 repair

A checksum or digest maps an arbitrary byte sequence to a smaller fixed-size value. Different families make different promises.

An additive checksum is mainly an accidental-error detector and is weak against structured changes such as reordering or compensating byte modifications.

A CRC interprets bits as a polynomial over GF(2)GF(2) and computes a remainder under a declared generator polynomial and parameter set. CRCs are excellent for many transmission/storage error patterns, but they are not cryptographic authenticators.

A cryptographic hash such as SHA-256 is designed so that finding collisions or preimages is computationally hard under the security assumptions of the primitive. A hash still does not authenticate a file when an attacker can replace both the file and the untrusted hash value.

SHA-256 compression structure

SHA-256 pads the message with a one bit, enough zero bits to leave 64 bits at the end of the final 512-bit block, and then the original message length modulo 2642^{64}. Each 512-bit block expands sixteen 32-bit words into a 64-word schedule and updates an eight-word chaining state through 64 rounds.

The important learning boundary is representation: message words are interpreted in the algorithm’s specified byte order. Reinterpreting native host integers without explicit conversion can produce a platform-specific hash implementation.

Known-answer evidence

tools/labs/crypto_primitives_lab.cpp implements SHA-256 directly and validates the standard digest of “abc” and the empty message. The same SHA-256 implementation is then used by HMAC, HKDF and a domain-separated Merkle tree.

This raises the evidence above “definition present,” but the implementation is educational. It is not reviewed for constant-time behavior, hardware acceleration, fault attacks, side channels or production cryptographic use.

What to use for what

Use a checksum/CRC when the threat is accidental corruption and the protocol specifies the polynomial/parameters.

Use a cryptographic hash when content identity or collision/preimage resistance is required.

Use a MAC such as HMAC when a party holding a secret key must authenticate content.

Use a digital signature when verification must be possible without sharing the signing secret.

Prerequisites

Bitwise XOR, Serialization, Endianness.

Used by

Integrity and authenticity, HMAC and HKDF, Merkle trees and authenticated structure, Production manifests and transactional publication.

Shader buffer ABI

Shader buffer ABI

A shader buffer is a binary interface between independently compiled code. CPU and shader code must agree on member offsets, element widths, alignment, array stride, matrix layout, and total record stride. “These structs have the same fields” is not enough.

Suppose a record logically contains a 3-vector followed by a scalar. The mathematical payload is four floats, but the ABI may impose an alignment boundary for the vector or the containing record. The only safe statement is the one established by the layout rules and, ideally, reflection/compiled shader metadata.

Layout is a function of context

Different interfaces can have different rules: vertex attributes, constant/uniform buffers, storage buffers, argument buffers and push/root constants are not interchangeable contracts. Matrix row/column-major convention is another independent dimension.

On the CPU side, standard C++ object layout also has rules about padding and alignment. Copying bytes from a native struct into a shader buffer is valid only when the native representation is deliberately made compatible or explicit serialization writes the expected offsets.

Verify rather than guess

A robust pipeline should generate or reflect a machine-readable layout description and compare it with CPU declarations:

  • expected offset for every member;
  • expected array stride;
  • matrix stride and orientation;
  • record size/alignment;
  • scalar widths and signedness.

Static assertions can catch CPU layout changes. Shader reflection or compiler metadata catches shader-side changes. A golden byte dump can test the complete bridge.

Failure modes

Common failures include using a 12-byte mental model for a vector type whose ABI slot is 16 bytes, mixing bool widths, assuming packed enums, copying pointer-containing structs, row/column-major disagreement, and updating one side of the interface without rebuilding the other.

Teach and reconstruct: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs#Make a shader record an explicit binary contract.

Related: Alignment and padding, GPU vertex specification, Tensor runtime layout and views.

TLB

Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C003 · Latest development: C003

Definition and mechanism

The translation lookaside buffer caches recent address translations and relevant access metadata, not the bytes being loaded. A miss may trigger a valid page-table walk without OS fault handling. A TLB hit can coexist with a data-cache miss. Context and permissions matter; it is not just a global VPN-only dictionary.

Prerequisites

  • Page tables and MMU — Cached or faulting translation starts from the mapping/protection mechanism.

Used by

Source and navigation

C003 teaching chapter · Part definitions · Dependency Map

Reconstruction depth

The Translation Lookaside Buffer caches recent virtual-page to physical-frame translations. Without a cached translation, the processor performs a page-table walk, which itself requires memory accesses and can stall an otherwise cache-friendly loop.

TLB locality differs from data-cache locality. A traversal can touch one cache line from thousands of separate pages: each useful access is small, but the page working set can exceed TLB capacity. Huge pages increase TLB reach because one translation covers more bytes, although they introduce allocation and fragmentation trade-offs.

When profiling, do not diagnose every unexplained memory stall as a TLB problem. Hardware performance counters can separate cache misses, page walks and TLB misses on supported CPUs. Synthetic experiments should vary stride and working-set pages while keeping useful work controlled.

For engine data, dense arrays often help both cache and TLB locality; pointer-heavy structures can hurt both. NUMA adds another axis: a translation may be cached while the physical page still resides on a remote node.

Multiscale texture filtering

Antialiasing and sample allocation

Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: XR01 · Latest development: Phase 10

Definition and mechanism

SSAA increases spatial observations; MSAA principally adds coverage-related sampling under its shading conventions. TAA reuses aligned temporal observations. Nonlinear shading makes pre-/post-filtering noncommutative, so coarse rates need appropriate input/output policies.

Phase 9–10 development

Antialiasing combines a sampling pattern with a reconstruction or integration footprint so unresolved variation contributes with controlled error. More samples can reduce Monte Carlo variance, while better placement can reduce structured error; these are different effects. Adaptive allocation based on observed samples changes the sampling procedure and can affect uncertainty estimates. Spatial sample allocation should remain distinct from importance sampling over path or event space.

Edge localization and subpixel contours

Edge localization and subpixel contours

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

An edge is a rapid image-intensity change, often associated with a material or depth boundary. Differentiating a noisy image amplifies high-frequency noise, so edge detectors first smooth with a Gaussian-like filter and then compute a gradient. Gradient magnitude estimates edge strength; gradient direction estimates the local normal. Nonmaximum suppression keeps a candidate only if it is a local maximum along that normal, thinning a broad response to a contour. Thresholding and hysteresis connect strong responses through weaker neighboring pixels. Subpixel localization fits a local peak to gradient samples, estimating a contour position between pixel centers. Accuracy depends on sampling, blur, contrast, and the assumed edge profile. This makes edge detection a measurement problem whose output uncertainty should propagate into later line, pose, or shape fitting.

Prerequisites

  • Convolution and filter footprints
  • Sampling aliasing and reconstruction

Learned image features and CNNs

Learned image features and CNNs

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

A convolutional neural network (CNN) learns filters that detect useful image patterns from data. A convolution layer applies the same small kernel at many image locations, so a feature such as an edge can be recognized wherever it appears. Early layers often respond to local contrast or texture; later layers combine these responses into task-specific patterns. Stride and pooling reduce spatial resolution, trading detail for computation and larger receptive fields. Training adjusts filter values by gradient descent using backpropagation and labeled or self-supervised objectives. Weight sharing gives translation equivariance: shifting an input shifts the feature map, but does not guarantee full translation invariance or robustness to scale, viewpoint, lighting, or distribution change. Padding and stride determine border behavior and output size; too much downsampling can erase small objects. A learned feature is a representation useful for a training objective, not a human-interpretable semantic guarantee. Performance depends on data coverage, augmentation, architecture, optimization, and honest held-out evaluation.

Reservoir resampling and ReSTIR

Reservoir resampling and ReSTIR

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

Reservoir sampling keeps a compact candidate for a weighted distribution without storing every sample. When candidate yiy_i has target weight wiw_i, maintain a running weight sum and replace the stored candidate with probability proportional to wiw_i; the reservoir records enough normalization information to estimate the desired integral without bias under stated assumptions. ReSTIR reuses candidates across pixels and frames, which is valuable when direct lighting has many possible lights or paths but only a few can be evaluated per pixel. Reuse requires correcting for the source and target distributions, accounting for visibility changes, and managing temporal history. If weights or normalization are wrong, the image may be biased; stale reuse causes trails or light leaks when geometry or illumination moves. The method reduces expensive samples rather than making sampling free. It depends on a valid estimator, careful normalization, and an understanding of whether correlated reused samples preserve the intended expectation.

Prerequisites

Sampling quality: stratification, quasi-Monte Carlo, and blue noise

Sampling quality: stratification, quasi-Monte Carlo, and blue noise

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10

Definition and mechanism

Sampling quality concerns the arrangement of points across dimensions used by an estimator, not only each coordinate’s one-dimensional histogram. Stratification partitions a domain and allocates points across cells, reducing large gaps for suitable integrands. Quasi-Monte Carlo sequences such as Sobol aim for low discrepancy and often improve integration of smooth, structured functions, though their samples are dependent and error estimates differ from IID Monte Carlo. Blue-noise point sets suppress low-frequency clumping while retaining local separation; they are useful in image sampling and spatial placement but do not automatically minimize every integral’s variance. Scrambling, domain mapping, dimensional ordering, and discontinuities affect performance. Compare methods against a clear target function and measure. The supplied probability narrative introduces stratification and Sobol but not blue-noise constructions; that part is an explicit teaching addition, not a received source claim.

Tensor-product interpolation

Tensor-product interpolation

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10

Definition and mechanism

Bilinear and trilinear interpolation apply one-dimensional linear weights independently along each coordinate axis. In a rectangular cell, each corner contributes the product of its axis weights; the weights are nonnegative and sum to one for coordinates inside the cell. This preserves the range of scalar corner values, but the interpolated surface can be twisted rather than planar, and derivatives may jump across cell boundaries. For a voxel field, trilinear interpolation provides a continuous in-cell estimate; differentiating it yields a local gradient, which need not have unit length even when samples approximate signed distance. Keep coordinates normalized to the cell and define behavior outside the sampled grid explicitly.

University course development

Radiometry distinguishes total radiant flux Φ\Phi in watts, irradiance EE in watts per square metre, radiant intensity II in watts per steradian, and radiance LL in watts per square metre per steradian measured with projected source area. A spectrum distributes the energy over wavelength; a three-channel RGB value is a measurement in a chosen color system and does not uniquely identify that spectrum. Solid angle measures directional extent rather than physical area. Consequently an area-light sample requires the projected-area and inverse-square Jacobian when expressed as a directional sample. Free-space radiance remains constant along an unobstructed ray, while irradiance from a point-like source changes with geometry. Photometry instead applies standardized visual weighting: luminous flux uses lumens, illuminance lux, and luminous intensity candela. These distinctions prevent treating brightness, exposure, flux and radiance as interchangeable scalar labels.

Random variables and probability laws

Random variables and probability laws

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10

Definition and mechanism

A random variable is a measurable mapping from outcomes to numerical values; its probability law describes how those values are distributed. Discrete laws assign probability mass to points, while continuous laws use densities relative to a chosen measure. A cumulative distribution function exists for either kind and records probability accumulated up to a threshold. Mixed distributions can contain both atoms and continuous parts. Density is not probability at an exact point, and it changes with coordinates according to a Jacobian. Expectation integrates a function against the law, whether the variable is represented by a PMF or PDF. These distinctions matter in sampling APIs: returned value, support, endpoint behavior, and reported density must refer to the same measure. A finite computer sampler approximates a continuous law with finitely many representable outputs.

Prerequisites

  • Probability spaces, events, and conditioning

Used by

  • Expectation, covariance, and dependence
  • Inverse, rejection, and importance sampling
  • Probability density and change of measure

Monte Carlo rendering estimators and variance

Monte Carlo rendering estimators and variance

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: Phase 10

Definition and mechanism

Monte Carlo integration estimates an integral by averaging random samples with importance weights. For target integral I=∫f(x)dxI=\int f(x)dx and samples drawn from density p(x)p(x), the estimator is Î=N−1∑k=1Nf(xk)/p(xk)\hat I=N^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^N f(x_k)/p(x_k). It is unbiased when samples cover every region where ff is nonzero and the density is correct. Its variance falls approximately as 1/N1/N, so halving standard error takes about four times as many samples. Importance sampling chooses pp to follow the magnitude of the integrand; multiple importance sampling combines strategies such as light sampling and BSDF sampling with weights that avoid overtrusting a strategy that rarely finds a contribution. Path tracing applies these estimators to light paths, while rare caustics and narrow visibility openings remain high-variance cases.

Phase 9–10 development

For independent samples from density pp, the sample average estimates the integral using terms f(Xi)/p(Xi)f(X_i)/p(X_i) where pp is positive on the integrand support. Unbiasedness requires the support condition and integrability; finite variance additionally requires a finite second moment of f/pf/p. A variance estimate describes sampling spread, not systematic bias. Dependent samples add covariance terms, and multiple-importance weights combine proposal densities while preserving mixture support. A confidence interval is justified only when its sampling and moment assumptions are stated.

Attention and visual transformers

Attention and visual transformers

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

Self-attention lets each token build a context-dependent mixture of other tokens. A learned linear map produces queries QQ, keys KK, and values VV; scaled dot products compare each query with all keys, softmax converts scores to weights, and those weights combine values. Multiple heads learn different relationships, while positional information tells the model where patches or words came from. Vision transformers split an image into patches, embed them as tokens, and process the sequence with attention and feed-forward blocks. Unlike a small convolution, global attention can relate distant regions in one layer, but its pairwise score matrix grows roughly as the square of token count. Patch size trades spatial detail for compute; positional encodings and training data affect transfer. Attention weights are a mechanism for mixing information, not an explanation of causal importance. A transformer still needs a task objective, data, optimization, and validation, and can fail under distribution shift or poor spatial grounding.

Contrastive vision and image-language alignment

Contrastive vision and image-language alignment

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

Contrastive image-language learning trains an image encoder and a text encoder to place matching descriptions near their images in a shared feature space. For a batch of paired examples, cosine similarities between normalized embeddings form a score matrix; a temperature scales the scores, and an InfoNCE-style cross-entropy treats the matching pair as the positive while other batch items act as negatives. The objective makes retrieval and zero-shot label comparison possible by encoding class names as text. It learns statistical alignment, not a guarantee that every phrase is grounded in the pixels. Batch composition, duplicate or semantically similar negatives, captions, and web-data biases all shape the representation. A model may associate a prompt with correlated context rather than the requested object, and similarity scores are not calibrated probabilities. Evaluation must distinguish retrieval, classification, localization, and reasoning rather than treating one score as general visual understanding.

Inverse, rejection, and importance sampling

Inverse, rejection, and importance sampling

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10

Definition and mechanism

Sampling transforms convert simpler random inputs into a target law. Inverse-CDF sampling maps a uniform value through a quantile function; rejection sampling accepts proposal draws according to a bounded target-to-proposal ratio; importance sampling estimates an integral by dividing each sampled integrand by the actual proposal density. Each method requires correct support and endpoint handling. Importance sampling is unbiased when the proposal covers every contributing region and the weighted contribution is integrable; finite variance additionally requires the integral of f²/p to be finite. Rejection sampling needs a valid finite envelope. Discrete floating-point inputs can hit boundaries that have zero probability in an ideal continuous model. Report the density with its measure and use the same measure in the estimator. A proposal that misses target support cannot be repaired by a larger weight.

Prerequisites

  • Random variables and probability laws
  • Probability density and change of measure
  • Stateful pseudorandom generators and stream state

Latin-hypercube sampling

Latin-hypercube sampling

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10

Definition and mechanism

Latin-hypercube sampling divides each coordinate axis into NN equal strata and uses a permutation so every sample occupies one stratum per dimension. With randomized within-stratum positions and randomized permutations, each sample has uniform marginal coordinates; samples are dependent by design. This can improve coverage for some integrands at arbitrary sample counts, including counts that do not form a square grid. It does not guarantee lower variance for every function, and IID variance formulas cannot be applied without accounting for dependence. Test exact stratum coverage deterministically, then compare estimator error over repeated randomized trials for the intended integrand. For N=5N=5, each axis still receives five strata, avoiding the missing-cell bias of taking five cells from a 3×33\times3 grid.

Stable probability normalization and log-sum-exp

Stable probability normalization and log-sum-exp

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10

Definition and mechanism

To normalize nonnegative weights, divide each by their sum; direct summation can overflow even when the normalized probabilities are representable. Scale by the largest weight before summing. For log weights aia_i, compute m+log⁡∑ieai−mm+\log\sum_i e^{a_i-m}, where m=max⁡iaim=\max_i a_i. Subtracting the maximum prevents exponential overflow, and the result can be used to form softmax probabilities. This assumes at least one finite, valid weight and requires an explicit policy for all-zero, negative, NaN, or infinite inputs. Underflow of very small normalized probabilities is a separate concern from overflow; do not silently equate zero after underflow with mathematically impossible. For log weights (1000,1001,1000)(1000,1001,1000), subtracting 10011001 keeps exponentials bounded while leaving the normalized probabilities unchanged.

Unsigned modular arithmetic

Unsigned modular arithmetic

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C001 · Latest development: C002

Definition and mechanism

Conversion and arithmetic in an unsigned NN-bit domain produce residues modulo 2N2^N; intentional wrap is valid, but wrapped bounds expressions can become security bugs.

Modulo m retains the remainder class after division by m. An unsigned N-bit domain uses m=2ᴺ: 250+10 becomes 4 when stored in eight bits, and 0−1 becomes 255. Narrow operands may promote first, so identify the operation type separately from the destination type.
