C002 teaching chapter · Part definitions and mechanisms · Dependency Map

From truth table to gate delay

A half adder adds two one-bit inputs a,ba,b. The sum bit is XOR and the carry bit is AND:

s=a⊕b,c=a∧b. s=a\oplus b,\qquad c=a\land b.

The truth table is not just a memorization device; it proves why one output bit cannot encode all four input sums. Input 1+11+1 produces binary 1010, requiring a second bit for carry.

A half adder has no carry-in, so it cannot by itself build every bit position of a multi-bit integer addition. A full adder incorporates carry-in and can be composed into ripple-carry or faster prefix structures. The important systems connection is dependency depth: in a ripple chain, each bit may wait for the previous carry, whereas parallel-prefix adders reorganize generate/propagate information to reduce critical path.

A reconstruction exercise should derive XOR/AND from the four rows, compose two half adders into a full adder, then explain why gate count and propagation depth are different optimization targets.

ONNX graph import and lowering

ONNX graph import and lowering

ONNX is a graph interchange format, not a command stream to execute blindly. Import therefore has two separate responsibilities: decode the normative serialized model, then lower its graph semantics into the engine’s own validated intermediate representation.

The ONNX IR describes a graph as a side-effect-free computation containing model parameters and a topologically ordered list of nodes. Node outputs obey single-static-assignment: an output value name is produced once. Inputs, outputs and initializers have declared types and shapes, and symbolic dimensions can constrain values across the graph.

Primary reference: https://onnx.ai/onnx/repo-docs/IR.html

Import pipeline

Parse. Decode Protocol Buffers into ONNX model objects. Reject malformed serialization before graph reasoning begins.

Validate names and versions. Check IR version, opset imports, graph name, duplicate names and unsupported domains.

Resolve value contracts. Establish element type, rank and known or symbolic dimensions for graph inputs, outputs, initializers and intermediate values.

Validate graph order and SSA. Every consumed value must either be a graph input, initializer or output of an earlier node; every node output must be unique in its namespace.

Normalize operators. Convert ONNX attributes and optional inputs into an internal operator description whose defaults are explicit.

Infer and verify shapes. Propagate shapes where operator rules permit it, while keeping an unknown dimension distinct from an invented concrete dimension.

Lower. Translate supported operators into backend-neutral internal nodes. Unsupported operations must produce a deterministic diagnostic, not fall through to an unrelated kernel.

Plan execution. Topologically schedule nodes, assign storage and lifetimes, select kernels by capabilities, and insert device transfers or fallback boundaries deliberately.

Why an internal IR matters

If Vulkan, Metal and CPU code each interpret ONNX attributes independently, the repository effectively owns multiple importers with multiple chances to disagree. The importer should instead produce one small semantic IR: tensors, operators, attributes, shapes, constants and explicit capability requirements. Backends lower that IR.

This creates a testable seam. A CPU reference kernel and a Metal kernel can receive the same normalized MatMul or Softmax node. Their numerical agreement can then be tested without re-testing protobuf parsing.

Executable graph contract

tools/labs/phase29_ml_runtime_lab.cpp does not parse protobuf and labels that limitation explicitly. It models the post-decode internal graph boundary and verifies that inputs and initializers are available before use and that node outputs satisfy SSA uniqueness. Negative cases reject use-before-definition and duplicate outputs.

That is deliberately narrower than ONNX support. Full support requires actual protobuf decoding, opset semantics, operator-specific validation, shape inference and numerical parity against a trusted runtime.

Related: Tensor runtime layout and views, Transformer attention and KV cache runtime, Interface contracts and publication.

Real protobuf and official reference-runtime witness

The internal graph contract is now complemented by tools/ml/onnx_contract.py, which uses the official ONNX package instead of modeling the interchange format by hand. The witness builds a ModelProto with MatMul → Add → Relu, named initializers and symbolic batch dimension, serializes it to a real .onnx protobuf, reloads it, runs the official model checker, invokes shape inference, and executes the graph with ONNX’s reference evaluator.

The expected numerical result is independently computed with NumPy before comparison. A second deliberately invalid model reuses a node-output name and must be rejected by the official checker, exercising the SSA constraint at the actual interchange boundary.

This changes the evidence level for the ONNX file/IR boundary, not for a production inference backend. Dynamic control flow, nested subgraphs, arbitrary opsets, external tensor data, quantized operators, custom domains, ONNX Runtime/device execution and current KairoONNX lowering still need separate proofs.

Transformer attention and KV cache runtime

Transformer attention and KV cache runtime

A transformer runtime becomes understandable when tensor shapes remain visible. For one attention head, let a token representation produce query, key and value vectors

q,k,v∈ℝd. q,k,v \in \mathbb{R}^{d}.

For a query attending to keys kjk_j, the scaled score is

ℓj=qTkjd, \ell_j = \frac{q^T k_j}{\sqrt{d}},

followed by a stable softmax

pj=eℓj−m∑teℓt−m,m=maxtℓt, p_j = \frac{e^{\ell_j-m}}{\sum_t e^{\ell_t-m}}, \qquad m=\max_t \ell_t,

and the output is

o=∑jpjvj. o = \sum_j p_j v_j.

Subtracting mm does not change the distribution because the same factor appears in numerator and denominator, but it prevents overflow when logits are large.

Causal masking

For autoregressive decoding at token position tt, a query must not observe keys and values from future positions. In a batch attention matrix this is represented by a causal mask before softmax. During incremental decoding, a correctly managed KV cache gives the same structural guarantee: only keys and values through the current token have been appended.

The cache exists because recomputing all earlier K/V projections every token is wasteful. If each layer has key/value vectors of head width dhd_h, number of KV heads hkvh_{kv}, sequence length LL, and element size bb, the rough storage per layer is

2Lhkvdhb 2 L h_{kv} d_h b

bytes before allocator and alignment overhead. Cache datatype, paging strategy and maximum context length are therefore memory-system decisions.

Multi-head and grouped-query attention

Multiple heads perform the same mechanism with separate projected subspaces. Grouped-query attention may use fewer key/value heads than query heads; the mapping from query head to KV head must be explicit. GGUF metadata commonly carries head-count and key/value dimension information, so model loading and runtime shape validation meet at this boundary.

Residual, normalization, and feed-forward structure

Attention is only one sublayer. A complete transformer block also needs residual paths, normalization, and a feed-forward network or architecture-specific alternative. The order—pre-norm versus post-norm, RMSNorm versus LayerNorm, activation and gating choice—is part of the model architecture and must come from the model contract rather than a generic “transformer” assumption.

Executable witness

tools/labs/phase29_ml_runtime_lab.cpp implements stable softmax and a small incremental KV cache. Two keys with distinct values make the weighting observable; a single-token case proves that incremental causal attention cannot see a future token that has not been appended.

It intentionally does not claim multi-head batching, rotary position embeddings, grouped-query attention, tokenizer behavior, paged KV caches, fused kernels or production-model parity. Those are separate implementation milestones.

Related: Tensor runtime layout and views, GGUF binary model loading, ONNX graph import and lowering, Quantized matvec and dequantization.

Why clipping a contribution changes the estimator

A capped weighted update replaces an unbounded contribution wxw x with something like

w̃=min⁡(w,wmax),Δ=w̃x. \tilde w = \min(w,w_{max}), \qquad \Delta = \tilde w x.

The cap protects an online system from one extreme weight dominating state, overflowing finite precision, or creating intolerable variance. But unless the cap is part of the intended mathematical model, it introduces bias: contributions above the threshold are deliberately underrepresented.

This trade appears in importance weighting, robust online statistics, adaptive reconstruction and control. The correct question is not “does clipping stabilize it?” but how bias changes as the cap moves and whether the uncapped tail is real signal, model mismatch, or corrupted data.

A useful experiment sweeps wmaxw_{max}, records variance, bias against an uncapped/high-precision reference, effective sample size and downstream failure rate. Tests should include weights exactly at the cap, negative/invalid weights when the domain forbids them, and extreme values that would overflow the uncapped path.

Full adder

Full adder

Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C002 · Latest development: C002

Definition and mechanism

Adds A,B,CinA,B,C_{in}; sum is three-way XOR and carry is the majority of its inputs.

A full adder adds A, B, and carry-in. Sum is their parity; carry-out is 1 when at least two inputs are 1. Build it from two half adders: add A,B, then add that sum to carry-in, then OR the two carry outputs.

Prerequisites

  • Carry and borrow — For N-bit unsigned addition, carry-out means the exact sum exceeds 2ᴺ−1.

Ripple-carry addition

Ripple-carry addition

Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C002 · Latest development: C002

Definition and mechanism

Each full adder feeds its carry to the next position, making worst-case circuit propagation depth grow with word width.

Connect carry-out at bit i to carry-in at i+1. For 01111111 + 1, a carry traverses the low seven stages. Circuit delay grows with width in this simple design; fixed-width software addition still counts as O(1) with respect to input size.

Prerequisites

  • Full adder — A full adder adds A, B, and carry-in.

Used by

GGUF binary model loading

GGUF binary model loading

GGUF is a binary container used by GGML-family inference runtimes. Treating it as “a file full of weights” is too vague for a safe loader. A loader must first establish a byte-level contract: magic, format version, tensor count, metadata count, typed metadata records, tensor descriptors, alignment, tensor-data offsets, and bounds. Only after those checks can tensor bytes become runtime values.

The first four bytes identify the format as GGUF. Multi-byte fields must be decoded according to the file format instead of reinterpreting an arbitrary file buffer as a C++ struct. Native C++ structs inherit compiler padding, alignment and host-representation assumptions that a binary file does not owe the process reading it.

A useful loading pipeline is:

  1. Read and validate the fixed prefix.
  2. Parse metadata key/value records with checked lengths.
  3. Parse tensor descriptors: name, rank and shape, data type, and relative data offset.
  4. Compute the aligned start of the tensor-data section.
  5. Validate every tensor interval against file length and arithmetic overflow.
  6. Keep file or mapping ownership alive for every lazy tensor view.
  7. Convert the file tensor type into an internal runtime type only after the descriptor is validated.
  8. Dispatch dequantization or quantized kernels from that internal type rather than from filename assumptions.

The official GGUF documentation describes the format as a single-file, extensible model container and defines architecture metadata, tensor data layout information, and attention metadata such as head counts and key/value dimensions. Those metadata values affect runtime shape contracts; they are not merely labels.

Primary reference: https://github.com/ggml-org/ggml/blob/master/docs/gguf.md

Prefix witness

tools/labs/phase29_ml_runtime_lab.cpp parses the GGUF magic, version, tensor count and metadata count from an explicit byte vector using checked little-endian reads. It has a negative case for invalid magic.

That witness intentionally stops at the prefix. It proves that the repository now owns the boundary between raw bytes and validated scalar header fields; it does not pretend that the entire GGUF metadata type system or quantized tensor catalog has already been implemented.

What a full loader must prove

A production reader must defend against truncated strings, absurd ranks, shape-product overflow, unsupported quantization types, alignment overflow, tensor intervals outside the file, duplicate or contradictory metadata, offsets that alias unintentionally, and files whose declared architecture cannot be executed by the runtime.

For memory mapping, “the pointer is valid” is not enough. The mapping object and file lifetime must outlive every lazy tensor view. Page faults also become part of performance: a model that technically maps instantly can still stall during first use if access order faults pages unpredictably.

Quantized execution boundary

GGUF storage type and execution type are separate decisions. A block-quantized format normally stores scale or other metadata together with packed codes. A portable reference path should decode or dot-product those blocks in a simple scalar implementation first. SIMD or Metal kernels then have an independent oracle. If the optimized path disagrees, the scalar path is evidence; if both paths share the same unpacking bug, the test is not independent enough.

Related: Tensor runtime layout and views, Quantized matvec and dequantization, Transformer attention and KV cache runtime, Binary format contracts.

Metadata and tensor-descriptor witness

The earlier prefix-only boundary has now been extended by tools/labs/gguf_metadata_tensor_lab.cpp. The subset parser validates GGUF v3 magic and counts, parses typed UINT32 and STRING metadata, consumes general.alignment, reads tensor names/ranks/dimensions/type IDs/relative offsets, computes the aligned tensor-data start, and rejects truncation or invalid alignment.

The parser remains deliberately incomplete rather than permissive. Unsupported metadata types are rejected instead of skipped with guessed sizes. It does not yet implement arrays, every GGUF value type, every GGML quantized tensor block, tokenizer metadata, endian conversion for big-endian files, or payload interval validation for all tensor types. That is the correct boundary for an independent reference: a small loader should fail loudly outside the subset it actually understands.

Quantized matvec and dequantization

Quantized matvec and dequantization

Quantization trades representation precision for storage and bandwidth. The runtime question is not merely “how many bits per weight?” It is what mathematical value each stored code represents, where its scale or zero-point metadata lives, and how the dot product is accumulated without silently changing the model.

For a simple symmetric per-row signed 8-bit scheme,

s=maxi|wi|127,qi=round⁡(wis), s = \frac{\max_i |w_i|}{127}, \qquad q_i = \operatorname{round}\!\left(\frac{w_i}{s}\right),

with clamping to the representable range. The reconstructed value is

ŵi=sqi. \hat w_i = s q_i.

A reference matrix-vector product can therefore compute

y=∑i(sqi)xi. y = \sum_i (s q_i)x_i.

That scalar implementation is not necessarily fast, but it creates an oracle for SIMD or GPU fused dequantization-and-dot kernels.

Before clamping, the scalar reconstruction error for ordinary round-to-nearest is bounded by roughly half a quantization step. The output error is workload-dependent because the dot product combines weight errors with input magnitudes. An accuracy report therefore needs representative activations or a model-level metric, not only weight reconstruction error.

Zero rows and exceptional values

When all weights in a block are zero, dividing by the maximum absolute value would produce an invalid scale. The format and runtime need an explicit zero-block representation. Non-finite input weights should be rejected or handled by a documented conversion policy instead of entering integer casts accidentally.

Groupwise 4-bit formats add another trade-off. Smaller groups let the scale adapt more locally but spend more bytes on metadata and may increase metadata bandwidth. Larger groups reduce metadata overhead but make each scale describe a wider distribution.

Reference versus optimized execution

tools/labs/phase29_ml_runtime_lab.cpp implements a checked per-row Q8 reference and compares its dot product against the original floating-point row under a stated error budget. The point is not to advertise Q8 as the final format; it is to establish the proof pattern:

stored codes plus metadata → scalar interpretation → reference result → optimized kernel → measured error and performance.

A Metal or SIMD kernel should be judged against that reference on adversarial widths, tails, zero blocks, extreme scales and random vectors. SIMD lane packing is an implementation detail; the dequantized mathematical contract remains the same.

Related: Quantization and compressed weights, GGUF binary model loading, Tensor runtime layout and views.
